utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor Djeric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will dwell only briefly on this pre-war period. Yesterday we established that on all three side -- or at least on the Serbian and the Muslim side there was good faith and an intention to lay the stress on economic progress and that was the reason why we had you in the government. The rest of the positions were filled mainly by professionals who were active in the previous regime.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. I'm not capable of speaking about this aspect because I hadn't taken part in the political debates. That was done by you and the remaining two sides. I only spoke about the segment in which I participated. That is, in the drawing up of the government plan for the period 1991-1995, and this programme was endorsed, if this is what you are talking about, then I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I wanted to say was that the Serbian component in the government consisted of Momo Pejic, Ranko Nikolic [as interpreted], Tatjana Starovic, all of them were professionals who were not political figures but were more people recognised within their respective professions?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me correct you. I think that Ranko Pejic was not a member of the government at the time. He joined us only later. He was not there at this particular time. Momo Pejic was there, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that Ranko Pejic was working in some of the government institutions such as secretariats or things?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. It is very difficult to catch up with your speed if you do not pause between the question and answer. Yes, Mr. Tieger, was that your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Precisely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Djeric, do you see the LiveNote which is scrolling upward? Now it's stopped. It means that is -- now -- you can start your answering the questions. That's one of the tips. But please bear in mind for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that disagreements occurred on the government intentions as well only after the SDA changed its orientation from the preservation of the Federation towards the course of cessation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're trying to draw me into some political matters, and I -- I can't sufficiently follow this or assess it. I know that there were some rifts in the government relating to the strengthening of the component of uniterisation within the government. This was particularly advocated by the Bosnian and the Croat sides and I can speak about that, and particularly I can speak about the issue of regionalisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that. Now I'm going to skip the subjects that have political connotations. I'd like to ask you this: Do you recall that the Serbian deputies from all political parties, due to the fact that a memorandum on the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina was adopted by vote without the required two-third majority and without the respect for our right to put a veto, they decided to separate themselves to a separate assembly within the same building but that they continued to work there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- that the government, contrary to the will and the vote of the Serbian component, on or about the 19th of December requested recognition from the European community although that could have only been done by the assembly in a proper constitutional way?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember those problems. I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that our political responses, including the forming of the ministerial council which was preceded by the forming, or rather the proclamation of Republika Srpska, that initially those were just moves that did not constitute any essential moves and that were merely responses to cessationist aspirations of the Muslim and the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree with you that these were merely manifestations as a reaction to the moves made by the other two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to the same analogy, was the Serbian Assembly, which took certain positions but did remain a part of the Republican Assembly, is it correct that our ministerial council of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina maintained and preserved this continuity, and that it was made up by nearly all representatives of the Serbian component in the joint government.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The ministerial council continued to work. It was formed, but at the same time all members of the ministerial council, whether they be ministers or deputies, continued to work within the joint government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The previous question may have changed intention in midstream, but as propounded by the accused was pretty much incomprehensible. More to the point: All the previous -- well, most of the previous questions have built in numerous components. I think the witness is doing his best to answer what he thinks is the general thrust of the question, but they are getting increasingly complicated and need to be simplified to be fair to the witness and for the Court to know exactly what part of the question is really being put to the witness and he is being asked to address.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's a request from the interpreters that both speakers slow down. Mr. Karadzic, I hope you under the pointer of Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency, I'm grateful for that. Since Professor Djeric knows exactly what I'm talking about, I am trying to summarise and shorten my questions in order to save time, but apparently this is counter-productive. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree then that these manifestations of ours were always prompted by something that came from the Croatian Muslim coalition despite the fact that we were participating in the government as a coalition?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can agree with you, but you see, these are all political matters, and you are more familiar with that. You knew more about that. I cannot speak about that in a competent manner. I can only speak about how we worked within the joint government and the problems that we faced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Do we agree, then, that these proclamations that we made of various bodies could have been abandoned had the historic Serbian Muslim agreement become successful and that our partners remained faithful to the Lisbon Agreement? We could have formed -- changed all these formations without any detrimental effects?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, it was possible to preserve peace had there been a wish for that. The Lisbon plan was a historic chance to preserve Bosnia-Herzegovina and not to proceed with starting a war. That's my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree that only after the 18th of March, when all three parties agreed on the Lisbon Agreement on the 24th and 27th March, we started a more serious process of the implementation of what was offered to us through the Lisbon Agreement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember these exact dates. I cannot designate them as some historical bench-marks, but I do know that on the basis of the agreements reached and the solutions arrived at within the Cutileiro Plan, we proceeded towards a kind of implementation of those instruments on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that the vice prime minister of the joint government was Mr. Miodrag Simovic, he was offered to become the chairman of the ministerial council, although he was not a belligerent person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know to whom the party offered certain positions. This is the first time that I hear of it, that he had been offered that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What I wanted to say was: Did you notice that we wanted to preserve the continuity of certain functions in order just to transfer them from the joint government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree on that. There was this initiative, and this initiative kept going in the future period. So the ministerial council became a kind of personnel breeding ground for all other future government authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that the continuity of our members of the Presidency was preserved and that Professors Koljevic and Plavsic continued to be members of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They continued performing their functions. There was no other solution because they were elected directly by the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree that when the government was formed you, although you were not a political figure or a belligerent person, we persuaded you, and you in turn persuaded other ministers to accept to lead the government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You offered me to become a prime minister designate, and I'm talking about you as the party. I accepted that, albeit it unwillingly, but times were such that was the context and I agree on that. As for the other part of your question, whether I persuaded anyone else, I didn't know do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But you said somewhere that people were not willing to accept it but they did accept it, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you know, later on. When the conflict broke out and so on, there were certain problems there. So the basis or the groundwork for the future government of the Republika Srpska was the ministerial council and that was a solution offered and implemented by the party. This is what I found as a ready-made solution, when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you of something that you said at the Assembly session, 12th Assembly Session of the Serbian People in BH.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] that's 65 ter 21, 44 -- page 44 in Serbian, and page 25 in English. Maybe we can call up this document for Professor Djeric to be able to follow this more easily. So page 44 in Serbian, page 25 in English; 65 ter 21. This is 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is where you start speaking. You say: [As read] "Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, deputies, it is only proper for a person to speak at this point. You have expressed your will. Your decision is as it is, and I shall not oppose it." So this has to do with your appointment; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then it says here towards the bottom: [As read] "I had certain dilemmas. Each of you probably has certain dilemmas and reservations regarding these times. However, there is one thing about which I had no doubts..." Can we have the next page in Serbian. [As read] "... the question of whether the Serb people or rather the Serb assembly needs a government at this point in time. I am deeply convinced that the assembly must have a government and that the Serb people must have a government, not for the reasons of cheap prestige or for the sake of pure form but because it is a basic necessity. "I would particularly like to warn you about several things which I consider relevant to the assessment of whether it is necessary that a government be formed. "First, you can see that it's not only the economic but also the national interests of the Serb people that are under threat. People are defending them, often spontaneously. You have to admit that the defence of the national interest must be articulated both at political and state level. One cannot allow all sorts of things to happen on the ground. There are also certain international as well as domestic laws, customs," et cetera. Do you agree that what you said and what the assembly did was after the Lisbon agreement had been agreed to; namely, the offer that had been made to us that we have our own constituent unit in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that. And that was done on the basis of the ideas presented in the Lisbon Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you do remember that already then we accepted to have a Bosnia outside Yugoslavia, to have its external borders preserved but internal decentralisation would be carried out on the basis of the provisions of the Lisbon Agreement, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at page 46 now, this same assembly meeting. 46. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can we scroll up. Or down. The previous page, please. I'd like to draw your attention to the paragraph that starts with the following words: [As read] "There is something else I have to say as well, something that I fear. The situation of Serb politics on the ground. This is a fact that even the political leadership of the Serb people find disturbing. This has to be overcome. We cannot have proper authority if everyone is going to establish some kind of authority according to some local criteria. We can only work on the basis of overall national interest." So was it already then that you identified this chaotic situation, and even our inclination towards excessive autonomy, small fiefdoms, did you already forecast that this would be a major obstacle in the functioning of a proper government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. This paragraph shows all of it. It is clear enough. The local factor was very influential, highly influential. For the most part, this is the result of the existential fear that prevailed among people then, as regards these state matters. So Yugoslavia was falling apart as a state or was in the process of disintegrating, so people were losing their state, and on the other hand even in this new state, which had already become an international subject, there was this outvoting in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm just clarifying what I had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say outvoting, are you trying to say that decisions are being made at the expense of one ethnic community; there is no security, there's a lot of improvisation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All important decisions then were made by outvoting. That is to say, on the basis of a coalition that was not based on proper principles. This was a coalition of the other two peoples, the other two ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. It became evident that there are different views with regard to how the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina should be set up internally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as this coalition is concerned, was the first watershed whether Bosnia would remain in Yugoslavia or whether it would leave Yugoslavia; and when we accepted that it could leave Yugoslavia but we said that it should be reorganised, then efforts were made to keep Bosnia as a highly centralised, unified state?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. Problems are linked to internal organisation. One side, that is to say, the Serb side, tried to give its contribution to decentralising the state, whereas the other two sides at the time advocated a strong, unitary centralised government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the previous system, which granted very significant powers to municipalities, they were mini-states in effect, all of that contributed to misunderstandings between the central organs and the municipal organs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, this is a question that would need to be explored, you see. Depends on the extent involved. It is true that people had gotten used to making their own discussions so that was a rather important consideration. On the other hand, the self-management system as such also gave a great deal of freedom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was saying that there was a great hope and a major chance involved. People could manage their own lives, govern their own lives within their small local communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to draw your attention to something that I said when speaking on a similar topic on the 24th until the 26th of July at the Assembly meeting of the SRBH.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 28, could that please be called. 28 is the 65 ter number; in Serbian it's page 14, English, it's page 17.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D92, Your Honours. And the previous one, 65 ter number 21, was Exhibit P96.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is my understanding that all assembly session transcripts have already been admitted, so we're not having anything admitted now. We would just like to have these documents shown. It's towards the bottom: [In English] "Essential problems we are facing." [Interpretation] I'm going to read it in Serbian. It's also the last paragraph on this page. [As read] "One of the essential problems we are facing is the poor functioning of the central authorities. The responsibility partly or mostly lies with us primarily because we have not fully defined the status of the SAO autonomous regions or their organs in relation to the central authorities; namely, fearing that we would be overcome or dominated by the Izetbegovic government, we prepared some political, not exactly state mechanisms, to resist abuse coming from the centre. Meaning that we inherited such mechanisms now that we have our own state. Now they return to us as a negative echo. We will all know immediately that this is about a Serb tendency towards autonomy, creating one's own principalities ruled by small scale princes behind which there is only private interest, never the interest of the people." Do you remember not only this particular speech but this problem that we had to deal with in the assembly? Because the establishment of the SAO gave an opportunity to local princes to do whatever was in their own interest.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. Every day that was being confirmed; namely, that the local factor want to rule on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 16 in Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then we're going to move on to 17.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in English, it's page 19. And it's the same document. I think it's around the middle of the page. It starts with the following words: "However ..." In English, it's page 19. 19 in e-court. And in Serbian, it's page 16. I'm going to read it out and then we're going to find it. So, again, I continue my address to the assembly. It says: [As read] "However, from an internal political point of view, we have enormous problems which this Assembly will have to define; i.e., to give a free hand to the Presidency and government to energetically carry out necessary measures in everyone stage. Now, at this stage the priority is to bring order into state mechanisms of power; that is to say, state organs: Reorganising the police for peacetime; placing the remaining police force within the JNA; placing all special police, which are being misused by some, under a single command of the republican MUP. By no means, under the command of some local lords." Do you remember that before the war the Muslim side enormously increased the numbers of the reserve police, 100 percent even, and more, and all of a sudden we faced that, that we had an enormous number of policemen?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we decided that this surplus should be resubordinated to the JNA, this is my old rhetoric, although the JNA had already withdrawn. So they should be resubordinated to the Army of Republika Srpska, and the ordinary police should just act as they usually do in peacetime, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that a month before this assembly session the Muslim side declared war on us and Serbia and Montenegro and that is how they defined their enemy. They said Serbia Montenegro and the Serbs in the SAOs, and a month after that we still wished to have a peacetime police?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot deal with the dates. Is this April? When is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is July. And it's on the 20th of June that they declared war, or rather an eminent threat of war. They declared war on Serbia Montenegro and us on the 20th of June, the imminent state of war had been earlier on.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the dates. But I think it was earlier. Perhaps it was earlier. Perhaps it was even the month of the April when the Ministry of Interior was instructed -- I mean, when Delimustafic issued this order for this attack. I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can agree with that. In fact, the war basically started with the directives of the 12th of April -- actually, the attack on the 6th of April and a few directives in April after that. However, formally war was declared, if you remember, on the 20th of June.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot deal with the dates. I cannot confirm the dates. Really. I do not remember. I mean, I can talk about what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can leave this document aside. Can we call up 1D5554 to remind Professor Djeric through this piece of news, to remind him what was going on. Most probably we don't have a translation. It probably hasn't been completed yet. Do you remember that the Presidency of the Serb Republic of BH, when the state of war was declared by the Presidency of the former BiH on the previous day, we wished to inform domestic and world public about the following: A state of war was declared and this is yet another confirmation that the Muslim and Croatian side is still in favour of a military rather than political option. Number 2, this war crime must be understood as an institutional pressure against the civilian population, especially citizens of Serbia ethnicity who are being forced to wage war against their brethren. Further on, Biljana Plavsic, as a member of the Presidency, says that she is against the fact that the state of war was declared. Has this jogged your memory a bit, in view of the dates?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. I remember. I remember the position taken by the Presidency in relation to this state of war that had been declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted for identification, rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2244, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't object, but I just want to note that this is one of the documents I believe about which we were not informed. In addition, there were an additional approximately 20 documents that were notified to us this morning, so we may be a little slow in catching up and may need some assistance during the process, but I don't anticipate objecting to any document on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, as to these background or the historical events, for example, declaration of war from whichever side, are you planning to file a motion for adjudicated facts or something like that in -- during the -- or before the Defence case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not an efficient way to deal with without having to deal with every witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, there already are many adjudicated facts about these issues, so to that extent we don't feel it's necessary to supplement them with adjudicated facts. But I noticed that during the Prosecution case they led a lot of evidence about things that were already subject of adjudicated facts, so I think if it's relevant we ought to be able to lead evidence; although, I agree that it shouldn't be a priority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Also, you also can think about the -- eliciting and agreed facts between the parties as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that would be useful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I recall well, we proposed an agreed facts list to the other side, but I'm afraid things got complicated along the way and we weren't able to reach agreement; although, I still believe we could agree on many things that are not directly in dispute. Can we go back to 65 ter 28. Page 20 in the English. And we have the right page in the Serbian version. 20 in the English. In the Serbian, we should stay with page 17. I'll read out so we'll try to locate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says local -- well, something was skipped. It says: [As read] "I would kindly ask the Assembly to once again consider the possibility that the deputies be held at the positions they are accorded as they are part of the highest level of authority in the republic. They cannot be suspended by any war staffs or War Presidencies. The deputies which created this state draft its law -- its laws that are -- ought to reflect the needs of the Serb people. They need to strongly support the legal authorities, especially in the municipalities where there are no war circumstances, as they can go on with their lives in a normal fashion. I must say that it is so under the law and international law," et cetera, et cetera. Do you recall that we even had to call upon the deputies to try and suppress such localist tendencies of different War Presidencies and war staffs. It was a problem both for the assembly and the Presidency and the government whose decisions were supposed to be implemented?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you just read out is a part of the document, and I don't want to comment upon that. However, I can confirm that there was always this insistence on the fact that Dr. Karadzic has mentioned; that is to say, the need for removing this strong local factor. I remember that the government issued instructions in which it stated that Crisis Staffs do not hold power and cannot hold power where regular bodies of authority can meet and work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that the Crisis Staffs were simply a way of concentrating executive authority in limited, areas as well as in such municipalities where the legal authorities were non-functional? The staffs of that nature were temporary organs which were put in place to speed things up, rather than going beyond their remit.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that they could not go beyond their scope of authority or to work in any different fashion than was prescribed by regulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that we understood quite early on that people no longer controlled -- or, rather, that they could not control the legislative branch and that we had to dispose of these Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We strove, both the Presidency and the government, to put the Crisis Staffs in a situation where they could hold power within their respective remit and in limited areas where they were necessary and not to work with any prescribed limits they assigned to themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Under the law and international law, it is stipulated that any decisions made by different Crisis Staffs and Presidencies are all considered to be measures decided upon in a state of war and do not have the same legitimacy as when a measure is pronounced by regular bodies of authority. That is why I would like to recommend to the assembly to confirm what the Presidency, in its activity as the assembly, to decide to appoint legitimate bodies of authority, civilian authority, and that it should function not in competition with the military authorities but in a complimentary relationship. Another important thing is that all para state and paramilitary need to be eliminated. At this moment, the para state formations are even a greater danger as they can make catastrophic decisions that nobody would even recognise in peacetime, ones that would only cause us great damage in the meantime. Was it your position, too, that such para state formations such as Crisis Staffs were ad hoc bodies which could cause great damage by virtue of their decisions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Djeric. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is not an appropriate form of question. First of all, it's impossible to distinguish the comment from what's being asked. Second, I don't know if Mr. Karadzic was reading from a previous document, but if not this purported question is embedded with commentary. And the objection I made earlier, to which Mr. Karadzic responded he was grateful for the need for -- to be advised of the need for focus, has been completely ignored, and now the questions are dramatically expanded and much more commentary is introduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very much so. Mr. Djeric, do you think you can answer the question or shall I ask Mr. Karadzic to reformulate his question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer in a simple way concerning this question, or observation. The local authorities, in many cases, took upon itself to have the power of regular bodies of authorities, and this is where the conflict arose. That is why it was constantly insisted upon such local authorities to be declared null and void so as not to have any power anymore. In general terms, that would be my answer to this observation or comment or question by Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the Serb page 18 and 19, and in the English, 20 and 21 so that we could see what you said at the same session on this topic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which session?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Between the 24th and 26th of July, 1992. In English, it's page 21. Perhaps can you find the paragraph I will be referring to. [As read] "It is well know that the government of the Serb Republic of BiH began its constitutional work under war-time conditions. In addition to facing a war situation, the government began working completely isolated and cut off from all sources of communication ranging from available institution, services, functions, information, means of equipment, technology, and staff. It began operating at the time when the system that had existed in the previous 50 years ceased functioning. This was at the stage when we were not economically, politically, or even psychologically prepared for what happened." Then further below, you say: [As read] "Its negative contribution was provided by the relocation of the government. Due to war-time circumstances and other factors, the government was completely blocked in terms of communication, contacts, and co-operation with the municipalities. The SAO Krajina and SAO Herzegovina were fully cut off from the government for a certain period of time and had no contact with the government." Do you agree that the government being cut off in terms of means of communication was a factor which only contributed to the strengthening of the local factors and it made the government feel as if its hands were tied?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I can add that the central authorities, given that the PTT network was based in Sarajevo, cut off all communications, so you can just about imagine how it was for the government to work under such conditions. As for the relocation of the government, I must say - although I don't know who decided on that and how it came about that the government ended up in Pale - I think in any case that at that point in time it was a major mistake. I don't know who decided on that, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to inform you, we had a lot of discussion about that, and we heard a witness from Ilidza here who testified that we visited that location looking for a suitable place, and we concluded that a single mortar shell could eliminate the whole government and that is why we relocated to Pale.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. So, we, the government I presided over, was completely cut off. There were no telecommunication means. There was no road or rail communication. There was no communication in any sense. It was practically impossible to work. Certain areas and regions became so independent in the meantime that it was difficult to establish any kind of communication with them, and that situation persisted for quite a while. Even after I resigned and left, some regions, I think, still did not fully accept the central authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 24 in the Serbian and 26 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is also your contribution before the assembly. You say: [As read] "Dear deputies, some of your positions, decisions, and conclusions, will be of special importance to the government's programme tasks and to the work of the government in the coming period. Therefore, the government asks the assembly to decide on the following proposals: "1. Reaffirmation of the constitutional guarantees of human rights and freedoms. That is, the option to accept all international conventions and agreements, which form the basis for asking for international recognition; "2. Strengthening of central authorities [as interpreted] to the extent necessary during war operations and the fight for freedom." Do you recall that this was one of the preconditions that was supported by the assembly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was way back, and I cannot recall it precisely, although I have no doubt that the government asked for this. It was my position then that we should honour the international conventions, agreements, and that we should have respect for the rights of citizens, human rights, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 25 in the Serbian and 27 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Again, your address, but item 7. [As read] "The government is also asking for support to immediately revoke all laws and other acts made by municipality, areas, and regions, or certain state organs which are -- which run counter to the constitution, laws, or other regulations of BiH Serb Republic." Do you recall that such laws were popping up everywhere and that you ask that they be brought in harmony with the constitution and the law?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I accept this as it is stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you accept that they were popping up all over the place because of the lack of communication and tendencies of autonomy?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I've discussed that previously, so I don't think you need -- I need to expand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Mr. Tieger on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. At transcript page 21, line 19, there is a reference to "central authorities." We heard in B/C/S "central government." We're going to ask that that be listened to, but I thought since we're going to be making that inquiry with CLSS, it's better to note that now in case it's something the accused wanted to raise again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just to confirm with the witness, that's part of your answer, Mr. Djeric, that sentence reads as follows: "Even after I left, some regions still did not fully accept the central authorities." Did you say "central authorities" or "central government"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to the highest authority in Republika Srpska. Because here we are talking about the government of Republika Srpska and the Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll leave it at that and we'll ask the court reporters to take a look at the recording of the hearing. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter 4214. It's D456. This is an assembly session held on the 14th and 15th September 1992. We need Serbian page 18 and the English page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read and hopefully we can find this portion. I am addressing the assembly. You can see that. It says: [As read] "We need to reinforce central government and" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Karadzic please indicate exactly where he is reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't follow where you are reading from. So could you start again, after indicating where it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is in the middle of the second paragraph. Line 10 or 12, exactly where the cursor is now. "In order for this to happen" -- now, yes, that's exactly the line I need in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [As read] "As physicists would say" -- I'm talking about physicists here, you can see it in the English version. "As physicists would say, we must ensure feasibility of this decision without any resistance in the conductors and resistors. The biggest obsession of physicists is to discover a super conductor. These conductors transfer all the energy they receive without any resistance. We must build such mechanisms that the decision of this assembly, the government, and the Presidency do not meet with any resistance, to implement them and achieve an effect on the ground in the shortest time possible and with the biggest effect possible..." Then I go on to say: "Knowing us Serbs" -- But let me ask you this: Can we say that still in December, the lack of these transmission mechanisms from the central government, the assembly, and the Presidency was still a burning problem?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the situation that prevailed in September as well, but even over the summer the government kept pointing out this problem from the very beginning, not only in September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I didn't know if Mr. Karadzic misspoke or if it was misheard, but the document we're looking at is a September document. I presume the reference to the September in the predicate to the question, but it was listed as December so I just was -- I was rising for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure I said September. Now let me go on by quoting: [As read] "The impressions about the Krajina are still vivid among the secret services, and there are attempts every day to bypass the BH central authorities; that is, the authorities of Republika Srpska. Attempts are made to pass things through -- to pass through things which might encroach on our sovereignty through commanders and municipal presidents." You would agree that that was another problem after we had abolished SAO Krajina, that this tendency survived; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, this is more your position, the position of the Presidency and the president. It's a political point of view, and I cannot either speak of it or put it in the right time-frame. All I can say is that this problem persisted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move now to another subject.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Can we have now 65 ter 22 -- or Prosecution Exhibit P1354. We're -- shall go back to the assembly meeting held on the 24th of March, 1992. Can we please have the Serbian page 5 and then we'll move on on page 6, and the page in English is 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are addressing the deputies here by saying: [As read] "We cannot finish our business today completely, only partly. In the meantime, I conduct in consultations and I consulted the presidents of SAO, and at the moment can I propose two candidates for two departments, and these are: Professor Doctor Minister Buha, which was followed by an applause; and the Minister of the Internal Affairs Mico Stanisic, which was also followed by an applause. "I am sure that you know these two candidates. These two people contributed greatly to the affirmation of the Serbian national interest in these difficult times. "I would like to underline that both candidates surely appreciate the situation in which the Serbian people are. I can't say that they refused this nomination and by Friday we are going to acquire and receive opinions." Can you confirm that Aleksa Buha was a prominent professor of philosophy, who studied in Germany, who speaks German and French, and that he was a respectable figure?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning what I said here is probably correct. But what is more important, though, is that -- I have to divide my answer to your question in two parts. Firstly, speaking about Stanisic and Buha, I proposed them and nominated them at Mr. Karadzic -- Karadzic's personal proposal. I don't have any doubts that the personnel commission was consulted previously and that they gave their opinion in that respect. He gave me those two names, and, hence, I gave these names at the assembly because I assumed that the party that he led had had appropriate consultations at grass-root or other levels, and I didn't go into that at all. I didn't know them quite well, but I was aware of their political engagement. I didn't have any reason not to respect the political power -- party. The only political party that was in power, and I went along with their wishes. As for the other part concerning these candidates, when I said that the assembly knew them, what I was referring to was that it had been agreed that members of the ministerial council of the Serbian Republic of BH would be the basis, or the basic personnel pool from which the government is going to be formed. And at that particular session, only two ministers were appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Obviously you had no contacts with the police because Stanisic in the post-election period was the chief of police of Sarajevo but he was rather inconspicuous, and do you agree that police chiefs should be inconspicuous?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him well. Had I known him well, there wouldn't be any way for me agree to his nomination, but since I didn't know him well, that is how these proposals were made.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have now 65 ter 5587. This is an assembly session held on the 12th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that on that occasion we changed the name of the state to Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if that happened on that particular session, but it is possible that it was in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 36 in Serbian and 38 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, you already presenting all the ministerial positions that have been filled. And you say: [As read] "I suppose that you are tired. And this intervention concerning the reshuffling of the government, I am going to make short as possible -- as -- as short as possible." So this is the first reshuffling of the government that you conducted in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we should say that by the end of April or early May, the government was already complete. There were several new names as compared to those who had been members of the ministerial council. So you cannot establish a full coincidence between the government and the ministerial council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor Djeric, do you remember that some of them returned to Sarajevo? Ranko Djuric decided to remain in the Muslim part of Sarajevo and so did Miodrag Simovic, so those were, among others, the reason that you had to change some of the members of the ministerial council?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I agree to that. But that was much earlier. That was in April or May. Simovic used to leave Sarajevo and then decided to go back. Tatjana, as well as many others, did the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was up to them to decide.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were free to decide whether they would accept it or not. Some of them I never even saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that, do you recall that Mr. Simovic rejoined us and was given a very significant position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now, I don't think this is exactly true. Initially he left and then he went back, so you could have talked to him during that interim period, but I didn't talk to them; therefore, I cannot say anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But towards the end of war, he came to Republika Srpska and he is currently the president of the constitution ideal court of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that happened later. It has nothing to do with me. I was a part of the care taker government, and I was not following all the comings and goings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Can we with have page 37 in Serbian and 38 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Item 3, you said: [As read] "The minister of health, work, and social protection, I propose Mr. Kalenic who has led this ministry so far." Do you remember that at that time Kalenic was from the independent party called Independent Democrats and previously they were called the Reform Forces?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that he was a member of the Reform Forces Party, and if I remember correctly, you personally were in favour of having such a personality as member of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 38, in Serbian, item 11, you propose that Professor Aleksa Buha remain as the foreign minister. That's page 39 in English. Do you remember that another opposition leader of the party called the Federal Party, and his name was Dragan Djukanovic, also became a member of the parliament?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Of the government.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that was after I had left. But it is true that he was a minister. While I was in office, Kalenic was the minister. He remained there. But this person came after me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I remember that you stated that you would be brief as regards these background matters. I'm really struggling to understand the relevance of these lines of questions, particularly regarding the political appointments, et cetera. I think -- it's -- it's time to come to more relevant issue, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, this witness is invaluable because he saw for himself and he participated in a very hard way in those initial attempts to regulate the state, the structure, the legal framework, and it has a lot to do with his amalgamated statement when we speak about the relationships within the government itself. All those participants could have been good individuals per se, but it was impossible for them to work well together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under item 13, you propose that the minister of defence and the minister of the interior, Colonel Subotic and Stanisic respectively, continue staying in their offices.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We tried to reshuffle the government. What you are talking about is exactly that, and we wanted to focus on some serious issues. It was not possible for me to agree with you about the reshuffling of the government and therefore, quite simply, we had to keep some of the solutions. You did [Realtime transcript read in error "did you"] not accept to have Mandic and Stanisic removed from their position. And that applied to other positions as well. There were some weaker positions; for example, the minister of the military. You know very well that this particular person was not accepted and approved by the army, and this question dragged on and on. And I was helpless. I couldn't do anything about it. But how can it be possible for a minister not to be accepted? These are complex things that I cannot go into in any detail at the moment. As I said, this was one of the attempts to reshuffle the government which failed and that is why some its solutions remained unchanged. As the president and the president of the party and the Commander-in-Chief, if you had quite simply realised and agreed that I was facing huge problems, the things might have taken a different course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us see what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So I was against any kind of dramatic dismissals, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, just a LiveNote issue. I think it'll be addressed when the transcript is cleaned up. At page 30, line 21, it reads: "Did you not accept not have Mandic and Stanisic removed." I think the witness clearly said, "... and you did not accept to have Mandic and Stanisic removed." I think that's -- I think everyone heard that and I think it will be probably cleaned up in the final version, but I needed to note that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be looked into by the reporters, I take it. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic. Could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that -- or rather do you remember that I was opposed to dramatic dismissals, but I did not oppose reconstructing the government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not the case. You were against having these two replaced, these two who were key people in the government, the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of Internal Affairs, especially because the government had its own programme from day one. So you can see in the minutes of government sessions, these are proper documents, you will see that the government insists on the rule of law -- honouring the rule of law. The government worked on institutionalisation on a passing laws, different measures, et cetera. They also wanted this authority to be felt on the ground. This was at the early stage, perhaps the end of May, beginning of June, that we started an appropriate procedure for establishing whether war crimes had been committed and whether there were any other violations of the law. All kinds of violations. Not to go into all these other matters involved. So this was at a very early stage. We wanted this procedure to be started. You see, whenever there is a war going on, people overstep. The government hears about this. There are also diplomatic letters that have been coming in. You know, all of this sort of spurs you into action, and I made every effort to have this done. It's not that I know. I mean, it's not that I am a witness, but, anyway, I did this with good intentions to start a procedure, to follow operations to see when people were going beyond the bounds that are there on the basis of international law. When people were overstepping, they should be punished. That's why these two ministers were so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at page 53 now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger. 23 ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I object to the witness being cut off, particularly at an obvious point when -- when something significant was being discussed. He had gotten to the point saying "that's why these two ministers were so," and then he was cut off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, please -- if you haven't completed, please continue. We didn't hear after you said: "That's why these two ministers," I take it those are Mr. Mandic and Stanisic, "was so --" What did you try to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, these are two ministries of particular importance, and it is important who are the office holders there in view of the tasks that these ministries have. And it has to do with regular government work. And it has to do with the government programme as such. So the government started this at a very early stage, establishing whether war crimes had been committed and punishing war crimes. This was the end of May or beginning of June, perhaps. The government started establishing military prosecutor's offices and military courts, and people were dragging their feet there as well. I don't know why, but you can see that there are obstructions. Further on, very early, very early, we instructed Minister Mandic and the Ministry of Justice - so it was the government that instructed him - to prepare a report about -- well, these legal dimensions if you will, regarding many questions that are related to war and the consequences of war and so on. Inter alia, I remember this had to with prisoner exchanges, you see; who is a prisoner of war, who is treated as a prisoner of war, then also how the civilian population is dealt with. All of these things were things that the government asked the minister to deal with, but the minister was dealing with something different, you see. Irresponsible, you know. You can't find him. He doesn't come to attend sessions. I kept saying that to the president all the time. I kept warning him. I think he was then the president of the Presidency. I think Dr. Karadzic was either the president or the president of the Presidency. I cannot remember now. But he was president of the party at the same time and he was also the commander of the army. So he was a person who did have powers. All of this had been put to him. So at a very early stage, practically from the beginning of June onwards, there was this problem of communication that I had. I, as prime minister, with -- well -- well, the president. President Karadzic, right, at the time, and Krajisnik, and so on and so forth. Because they were the Alpha and Omega of that government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I did not have the impression that I had cut you off, however the interpretation had not finished because you said those two ministries were important to me then. So "important" was probably missing from -- from -- well, so did you feel that you had been cut off or did you finish what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a certain sense, I could have stopped at that point but I also could have continued, and that is why I felt it was necessary to say what I said. And now you can assess whether this ask a natural continuation or whether it is something that sort of sticks out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, would this be the right time to take a break, or shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will have a break for a half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please go back to this document again. That is to say, 65 ter 5587. And then in Serbian, it's page 53, and in English, it is page 54, and then we're going to move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I was just going mention this before - and I think Mr. Karadzic has been generally doing that - if in addition to the 65 ter number if we can identify the date of the document, particularly if it is an assembly session, it makes it much easier to retrieve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That would be helpful. Yes, I agree, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's Exhibit D422.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it's the same document. The same assembly. The 12th of August. However, I will observe that. It's going to be easier for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. This is your own address, and you say: [As read] "Gentlemen, deputies, the government's cabinet is one of a collective effort. In this, or in some other case, you have authorised the prime minister designate or the prime minister to propose he -- the persons he is going to work with." And then further down it says --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you also scroll down in Serbian. I believe that in English we need the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The assessment. What you are saying is the assessment is that the time is not right for any radical changes, that includes me as well. As regards Mr. Subotic, it is true that according to the decision we reached at Mount Jahorina, which the intention of enabling the reshuffle, all the ministers voluntarily signed to be on disposal. No personnel changes or additions of any kind could have been made if they had not done so. However, quite apart from that, I propose that Mr. Subotic, regardless of the fact that he is, due to this or that reason, ready to continue his work until further notice..." So do you remember these words of yours, that you also agreed to this, that these dramatic moves should not be made and basically ministers signed up to that. They basically said that they were at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can start now. What I said, you see, well, quite simply, there was this pending issue of the government reconstruction. That problem had been there for a while, basically between the Jahorina assembly that is being mentioned here and this assembly meeting in August, the one that this transcript is from, if I understand things correctly. So the problem of reconstructing the government had been there for quite a while. That is why I asked the ministers to resign. However, I did not get the consent of the political echelons. That is to say, Karadzic is the key person there; the Presidency. So the only thing that remained was to have things end the way they did. Quite simply, they did not agree to have the government reconstructed. That was the reason for this address of mine. That is why I spoke the way I did. You know that political support is required for reconstructing a government, and I did not have that at the time. Many ministers would have been replaced. Many. It's not only a question of these important ones. That was the priority. But, you see, that even the minister of defence is being mentioned here. Also some others who had economic portfolios and so on. However, I did not receive support, and that's the key.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. However, Professor Djeric, do you agree that although they all tender their resignations, the reconstruction had to be discussed at the meeting of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that out of 83 deputies in the Assembly of Republika Srpska, there were only 13 or 14 opposition MPs from different parties. All the rest were SDS deputies.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that because I was not really involved in such statistics. How many MPs there were from which party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But you can agree --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I can take your word for it here. But I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. That's easy to establish. However, do you agree, for instance, that among these 13 or 14, there were reformist, socialists, former communists. Then in addition to Dodik there was -- there were some other communists, socialists, there was one from the SPO; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I confirmed that when you asked me before, that in parliament there were representatives of other political parties or orientations too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let us look at page 64 of this document. And page 65 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the words of the presiding officer. The answer to that question should be provided by the corps commands and General Gvero will be there tomorrow." But that's not so important. Can we discuss the cabinet composition as proposed by Mr. Djeric who is in favour. It seemed to me not everybody voted who is in favour. Thirty-six are in favour. This is not sufficient. Who is against? Five are against. Did anyone abstain? Fourteen. So this means we haven't reached a decision now. I must conclude that this may be called government crisis as they say in the west. What does it mean now? It means that we haven't elected a government cabinet and that the government is about to resign. They will keep on working until the next elections." Mr. Djeric, can you tell me who were the 36 who voted for you, for your proposal?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't. There's no way for me to know who the 36 were, who voted against or for. In any case, it seems that this dispersion of votes addresses what the MPs knew. In other words, everyone was aware that there was a problem in the government and that certain ministers cannot be replaced as there's no political will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were only short of six votes to reach the figure of 42; correct? And, if by definition, the opposition usually abstains, then, Professor Djeric, we need to conclude that the 36 were SDS MPs, and I presided over that very same SDS, and yet they voted in favour of your proposal.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. But the problem was not resolved. The problem remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a problem, since you did not agree to the government being restructured. You did not led your political support and everything was up to the government, which, in and of itself, had a big problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll discuss further what my behaviour was. But do you agree that I did not lend support -- or had I not lent support, these 36 SDS deputies would not have voted in your favour? If you think I didn't fight it, I agree. But do you agree that a politician cannot fight battles he may lose. In other words, he cannot stand up to the parliament; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, these are different matters. Party matters. And the matters of the president. I won't go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 65 in the Serbian and 67 in the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your words: [As read] "Gentlemen, the government collapses if the assembly gives a vote of no confidence and not because of the problems with some candidates or similar things. That is the rule, and it is well known. So it happens if the assembly gives a vote of no confidence in the government." You completely followed the tenor of the constitution and the Law on Government; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 68 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here we see Mr. Buha, another university professor and minister of foreign affairs, address the assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you wait till we have the problem English page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 70 in the English. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbian, it is line 7 of his contribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [As read] "As a member of the government" -- or, actually, just before, he says: [As read] "It's the most normal thing to give a vote of no confidence to the government. The assembly and the deputies are the ones to evaluate the work of the government. As a member of the government, as of this moment on, I feel like a man who has been given a vote of no confidence, but I am also ready to carry out my work in the best way like I had done so far until the next government is chosen. I wasn't concerned with any changes of government, ministers, prime minister. On the contrary, I think it is a good sign. I have a feeling that something is wrong in the work of our government. I can't identify it, but it must be resolved, and I don't know of a better way to resolve it than what we have done this time." Then further below, he says: [As read] "I am in favour of putting a stop to this discussion and to accept the results of the vote and conclude that the government hasn't received a vote of confidence by the parliament and that it is obliged to continue working until the next session of the assembly when a new or the old prime minister will be offered a mandate and when the new government will be formed. Maybe it is going to be the same government and yet it may be a completely different one. Maybe some people from this government will remain, but it remains to be seen." Do you recall this contribution by Professor Buha?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a while, but I have no reason to doubt that it was said the way it is in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, this is an audio-recording that was transcribed. Can we go to page 74 in the Serbian and 76 in the English. Let's see what one of the ministers had to say as his position was discussed as well. Mr. Mandic says towards the bottom of the page: [As read] "If there was a vote of no confidence, then, gentlemen, it means that until the next assembly session, the Presidency of the Assembly ought to elect a new or old prime minister designate who will then propose his new cabinet. I think our colleagues need to explain that. The present crisis of the government -- well, the new cabinet and prime minister were not accepted. The mere fact that none of the candidates were accepted into the cabinet means that the entire cabinet falls as well as the prime minister. The old government is going to work until a new government is elected," et cetera. So it seems that everyone in the government was on the same page, including the prime minister and the ministers. In other words that unless there was a vote of confidence, the government ought to fall as it had not received assembly support; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But then particular responsibility is on the president, who needs to ensure that the constitutional order is functioning. Also the Speaker of the assembly and party president. In other words, it created an opportunity for you to show -- or, rather, to secure the functioning of the constitutional order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But do you agree that this was fully legitimate and that many SDS deputies voted in your favour?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is not in dispute. We've just confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to 65 ter 2 -- no. 4214, which is D456 dated the 14th and 15th of September, 1992. In the Serbian, page 11; in the English, page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at what Minister Subotic said. It's towards the bottom in the Serbian. We have the right page in the English. Subotic says: "Honourable deputies, Mr. President, I attended two or three military and political consultations which were attended by the presidents of municipalities from all regions, unit commanders, commander of the Main Staff, with us on behalf of the government, as government representatives, several of us ministers, and the president of the republic. The explicit conclusion at all those consultations was that our authorities were not functioning. "You will remember a few days ago in Bijeljina you adopted the same conclusion and I expected some of you to at least say something about it and make a proposal to the assembly. I think that you adopted this conclusion, Mr. Kupresanin, as far as I recall. "Therefore, I propose broaden item 71 so as to include the functioning of authorities in the Serbian republic and the restructuring of the government. I also propose to set forth problems regarding the functioning of the authorities from the municipalities to the government and the highest organs in the Republic. "We should discuss these matters as part of this item and decide on what to do in future." So we still have the government crisis, and between the 12th of August and the 14th of September, no new prime minister designate was appointed.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that I was in no rush to appoint a new designate, expecting that you might withdraw your resignation, whereas you stated later on that you did not wish to do so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably interpreters didn't hear you answer because it overlapped with the question. Did you answer the question, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was waiting for the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- so that I can then start answering, given your caution of before. I cannot agree with you, as you make a connection between your stalling or dragging your feet when restructuring the government with awaiting for my resignation. The assembly did not offer a vote of confidence and there was no need for you to wait for my resignation. You kept dragging your feet endlessly, and then the Prijedor Assembly session arrived and I had to finally cut the knot, so I offered my resignation in writing. I didn't even have to do that as the government had already received a vote of no confidence. I couldn't work but everything was being dragged on endlessly, and we were constantly in a legal limbo. Therefore, I even had to make this last move and say I won't keep up with it any longer. I offered my resignation in writing. I said that I would no longer be a prime minister of a government which is not functioning. There was this situation of stalling, and I refused to bear with it any longer, to put up with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that not only in this case of the government but only in many other instances I was very much against any sudden moves, and you agreed with me that dramatic moves should not be made?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
