utterances.text: Well, you see, the responsibility was upon your shoulders, the political responsibility. The fact that you were not in favour of dramatic changes at that point in is a matter of your political assessment and the assessment of the political leadership. I won't go into that. That was your right. But I'm simply trying to say that it had a negative consequence on the work of the government and the legal situation as a whole. Of course, the one bearing all responsibility is the one making the political assessment, in terms of whether a new government needs to be constructed or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 17 next in the same document. In English, it's page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will start reading and probably we'll find it. Karadzic says the following -- we can see that on the previous page. Well, we can go to the previous page to see who the speaker is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbian, it's page 17, I believe. I don't know if it's the same page in e-court though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's go back until we see whose contribution it is. Is this the right one? It's in the Cyrillic script, but can you see well that it is my name; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 17 in the Serbian then. Page 15 in the English. The bottom half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I say: [As read] "We'll have to be emphatic as members of the government. We will have to be forceful as members of the government and the Presidency. We must visit municipalities and restore order, even at the risk of introducing extraordinary measures, making replacements, arrest, appointments, and naming others who, with the help of deputies, will be able to pull the municipality out of a crisis. I think that tomorrow we will devote a lot of time to the restructuring of the government, how it should function and how to implement adopted decisions. I am certain that the government has done a lot already. If we look at all the legislation that has been adopted, it may be concluded that a lot of work has been done, but the question now is to ensure the implementation of those decisions." Do you remember that the government, indeed, proposed many laws and other decisions to the assembly that the assembly needed to approve, and the government, in and of itself, issued a number of regulations and made a number of decisions within its purview?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope that by the end of your testimony we shall be able to see the Official Gazette which shows that during your term of office as the prime minister, on the average, five to seven enactments a day, including Saturdays and Sundays, were adopted by the assembly. So it was a 24/7 operation, wasn't it? But the problem was how to effect the implementation. I said on many occasions that the bigger problem is how to implement all of this on the ground, rather than that there was a problem with the government itself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might agree with you that, indeed, the government at that time worked on a daily basis. One can say that they were in permanent session. There was not a single day that we didn't work on the institutionalisation of the system. As I said earlier, we had this problem of implementation that we faced on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move to page 141 of this same document; and 130 in English. Can you please enlarge this for Professor Djeric, this portion where he speaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you say here: [As read] "We stayed long into the night last night until 5.00 and discussed problems involving the work of the government and the conditions it was working in. We agreed that the location where the government was working was disputable, that it wasn't the best solution, but it decided that should remain there for a while as long as weather permits and we'll discuss the matter then." So, at that point you spoke about weather conditions. That is the time when the government was sitting in Jahorina where, during winter time, there is a lot of snowfall - is that right? - and you decided that, weather permitting, you would remain at Jahorina but that a solution would be sought for; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that the government was at Jahorina at that time. However, I don't know which session is this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 14th to 17th September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we are talking about the assembly, aren't we? So, please, I don't consider this to be a particularly important issue. It is true that the government was sitting in Jahorina in difficult conditions, and this is not an important issue that had an impact on the lack of the functionality and the impossibility to implement the decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Djeric, it is important for the Chamber to know that you were sitting on top of a high mountain, that you didn't have any means of communication, and that it was difficult for you to reach Pale through heavy snowfall?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The elevation is over 2.000 metres. It is good for skiing. But that was the only place because there were hotels there, and that was the only place where the government could sit. There was no better place in this whole area than the one on this summit which was more than 2.000 metres. As I said a minute ago when I spoke about the relocation of the government to Pale, I didn't mean that at that time I didn't think it was a good solution, but it was simply the consequence of the whole situation that this was done. But I don't see this as the crucial problem that caused the bad functioning of the government. I thought that ministers were more important in that context than this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you go on to say: [As read] "Concerning the reconstruction, we conclude that this was not the time for an overall government reconstruction. It was now more important to fill up the vacancies in the government. Under the constitution and the law, the prime minister has the right to nominate a member or members who should be dismissed. "In a nutshell, I propose that we appoint Minister Aleksa Milojevic as the minister of reconstruction and development." Then you went on to nominate Milojevic and Erceg -- Vidojevic and Erceg, and Dr. Dragan Djokanovic, the minister for issues concerning veterans or victims of war. And we did agree, didn't we, that he was from an opposition party. And now you went on to say that Ministers Antic and Mandic be relieved of their duties so that they can prepare for their new duties and to keep them as ministers without portfolios. Then you go on to make another proposal to the effect that Ministers Ostojic and Kalenic be temporarily assigned to the Ministry of Refugees and Humanitarian Aid until we appoint a person to this point, and so on and so forth. Do you remember these proposals of yours?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I mean for the benefit of the transcript: Yes, I do remember this proposal, but I have an objection to the manner you are phrasing your question. You said here that there was a no vote of confidence for the government, but now you're taking me back to the period that preceded this vote. Therefore, I can say that I did not win your support or the support of the political leadership, and you personally, and I believe that Krajisnik played a major role in the whole process, but let's not go back to that. Anyway, I didn't receive any support to reconstruct the government, and, quite simply, you accepted that, for the time being, we fill in the vacant positions and -- is this the August assembly --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, it's the September assembly.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not get support for the reconstruction. We only got support to fill in certain positions, and, therefore, these proposals were made in order just to make the government operational.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. Interpreters didn't hear the question itself. And when you read out a document, you need to slow down, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I was just going to rise for that point noting that the court reporter as well has requested some relief from the pace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, Professor Djeric, I am following a chronological order. This was the 12th of August when the government was not accepted. You are right, I was trying to postpone the nomination of a new prime minister, but in this transcript you see that I commended the government for doing a good job but that the problem was the impossibility of the implementation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the answer due to overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters were not able to hear your answer, Mr. Djeric. Could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was told to look at the screen and to react when I see the question -- the letter Q.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. You should react to the letter A.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I'm still waiting for the A to appear. Can you please repeat the question because I lost it a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was the assembly of the 12th of August, when, by six votes only, your proposals with a not accepted. 36 were in favour. Then, as you put it, I was stalling, and this is your opinion; whereas, I think that I wanted to give time to heal up these things. And then in September, in the previous paragraph, we heard that I was highly appreciative of the business and job done by the government but that the actual problem was in the impossibility of the implementation of its decisions?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. You were entitled to have your assessments and your views, including a view that time is the perfect healer. But I didn't share that view because I always had in mind the responsibility that lies on the government. I was aware of the responsibility of the government and you cannot not leave it to time to heal everything. As I said earlier, there were some serious problems in the lack of functionality of the authorities that was imposed from the local level, but I also said that there were some internal problems within the government itself, specifically the performance of certain ministries and key ministers, and I insisted on that throughout the whole of that summer because some of the solutions were rather unfortunate, they were not good, and it was not easy to resolve them as you can see for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 142; and 132 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's towards the bottom of the page, where we have your contribution and you say: [As read] "Honourable deputies, you do have the right to ask questions and, in the previous procedure, to propose candidates as ministers. I say that you have a constitutional right because the prime minister or the prime minister designate, who is the prime minister in this case, proposes the dismissal of government members or appointment of candidates for vacancies in his cabinet. However, it is not standard practice to contest proposals made by the prime minister for a simple reason" --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move to the page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [As read] "... that he has the right to form his own cabinet and to be responsible for its work. If we pursue this practice, it would considerably diminish the responsibility of the prime minister and the government as a whole. I think it would be much better to adopt the prime minister's proposals and to have the assembly control the work of the government on the basis of the constitution and the law." Do you remember this statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a general statement and a statement given in principle that stems from the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. But, however, do you remember also that in the Law on the Government, the assembly is responsible for individual ministries and that the ministers are obliged to submit reported to the government, and then the government has to passes on these reports to the assembly for each particular department and then the assembly would give its own opinion on that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You are invoking the constitution. As far as I know, it is the government who reports to the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not referring to the constitution but, rather, the Law on the Government, which stipulates that the ministries are also responsible to the assembly, whereas ministers are independent in their work.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the moment I cannot remember what specific provisions were at the time and who maybe amended them, but if the government has the responsibility towards the assembly, I don't see any reason for the ministries to be parallelly responsible to the assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now can we look at page 146 in Serbian and 135 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, we have the speech by the Speaker or the president of the assembly. The third paragraph. [As read] "Now we have to relieve Momcilo Mandic from his duties as minister of justice. First we have it relieve him and then appoint him as minister without portfolio. "Are there any questions? "No. "Who is in favour of relieving Momcilo Mandic of the post of minister of justice? "We must vote. Who is in favour? "I would like to take a count. Thirty-one votes in favour? "Anyone against? "One against. "You did not all vote. Two voted against. Any abstentions? Ten abstentions. The proposal to relieve Momcilo Mandic from the post of minister of justice has not been accepted. Now we can't appoint him as a minister without a portfolio." Do you agree, Professor Djeric, that the 31 deputies by definition, even if those ten absentees were not opposition, we would still have 21 deputies from the SDS who gave you their support.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who is the president here? Is this the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, Krajisnik is the president.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why are you asking me about this vote? What does it have to do with me? Do you understand? So a proposal was made for Mandic to be replaced and the deputies did not vote in favour of that so he retained his position. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But what I'm interested in and what the Chamber is interested in is how I conducted myself. Look on -- out of the 43 deputies, 31 of my deputies supported you, two were against, and ten were absentees.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were not supporting you. They were supporting the idea of keeping Mandic in his place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But can you deduce that they did that according to my instruction? Because they did not support Mandic, they actually supported you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not about me. This is about Mandic. But why the deputies decided to keep him where he was and I, on the other hand, persisted of having him replaced, that's another matter. We have to see who and in what way made that possible and why the deputies voted the way they voted. It -- I really cannot give you an answer to that. You're asking me something that I don't know anything about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this is it quite simple, this position, Professor Djeric. So it's not that they supported him. Rather, there weren't enough votes for him to be dismissed, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the said person had influence. Now who ensured that influence for him and in which way, that I don't know. However, it is a fact that he performed poorly, that he was not working well, and we couldn't get rid of them. So he had some kind of connections, and I cannot establish who, or what.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yet again, please let us look at the results of the vote. It the is it only two that voted in favour of him. Ten abstained. And over 30 supported the proposal to have him dismissed but that was not sufficient out of the total number of deputies.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't, and that's quite clear. Now, put a question. How could the chairman, how could the parliament ignore the constant requests made by the prime minister to make certain changes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, do you see that 15 to 1 were in favour of the resignation or dismissal but that was not sufficient? So no one really wanted the deputies to protect him. On the contrary, only two protected him. But it wasn't sufficient to have a reconstruction of that kind. I wonder whether you had any information to that effect, that somebody was supporting him, when you see that you are the person who enjoys the support of the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What matters here is that what was requested was to have Mr. Mandic replaced. Do you understand that? So appropriate support was not received. You see, these are problems of parliament now. The problem of pursuing a particular strategic policy in parliament. That's a different matter altogether. What matters is that he stayed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll see until when he stayed on.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he stayed on until I resigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the new government did not include either Stanisic or Mandic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Let us try to cut things short, all these questions and so on and so forth. What matters here is that I stopped this torment. I signed this resignation in October at the Prijedor Assembly in order to bring all of this to an end because I didn't go into the functioning of the Presidency any longer, or of the assembly, or of the party, or of the top political echelons. Quite simply, I asked to leave. I didn't even want to have technical mandates any longer. What I always bore in mind was the assembly vote from the month of August, when the government did not receive a vote of confidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Let me finish. I resigned. I submitted my resignation in writing. That resignation was supposed to be received at that very same moment, at that assembly. And look at what happened afterwards? The resignation was not accepted. It was simply glossed over although it was submitted in writing, although there was nothing unclear about it. Then came the next assembly in Zvornik. That was the month of November. Now, at that assembly everything was well-known. I had submitted my resignation, so the gentlemen were supposed to prepare a prime minister designate. There was nothing unclear about that. Again, the same situation occurred at that assembly. My resignation was received but a new prime minister was not designated. So they kept dragging this on and I remained in the same position from August onwards. So then, by way of a demonstration, I simply asked to have nothing to do with it any longer. And the gentlemen took over the government from that point. These remains of the government. They found a deputy prime minister designate and they went on until the next assembly, whenever it was that that was confirmed. So let me try to cut all of this short. Obviously the Speaker of the assembly and the assembly had to be at a higher level, had to have a greater sense of responsibility, because when such matters are involved, one has to act in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the government did not get a vote of confidence, then a new procedure has to be embarked upon. There are no political or any other efforts to be made there. I mean, like with these resignations, with the ministers or deputies or preparing the deputies. I mean, I cannot go into the reasons now why certain deputies did not vote or did vote or why they abstained or whatever. I'm not going into any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, for reasons of principle, the opposition always abstains. They hardly ever support the government. That's the way it is everywhere, and that's the way it is today as well; right? Thank you --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is a matter that the theory of politics should deal with. But I don't think that this would be the right opportunity for me to say what the opposition was supposed to do or what the opposition actually did. It's not for me to say that. It wasn't really my job. And I don't think that I am here in that role now, as an expert for political systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 6328 now. That is the assembly session held on the 31st of October and 1st of November. And that is Exhibit P1468.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, Professor Mr. Djeric, do you understand that I was not pleased to have the prime minister changed and that I was stalling as far as the appointment of a new prime minister was concerned?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean -- well, for me to say something about this I mean, I really don't know what I would say. I mean, this is some feeling that a leader has at a given political moment. Now how he feels, was it easy for him, was it not easy for him. I mean, really. I cannot provide any comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 7 in Serbian and page 8 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just make clear for the benefit of the Chamber and perhaps the witness, unlike previous sessions this is not a stenographic record or a transcript of a tape-recording of the record. We only have the minutes of this session and not the full transcription of the discussions that took place. Just so that that's understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at (g). Is that part of the debate? It has to do with the functioning of the government, the Presidency, and the party. Many objections were raised in view of the work of the Presidency, the government, and the SDS. Particularly it was the local government that was criticised because they were obstructing principles that were supposed to be carried out in practice. What was suggested was to ensure proper exercise of government at all levels in the republic. And then a bit further down, it says: [As read] "During the session, a group of MPs submitted a proposal in writing to have a vote of confidence in the government. At the same time, the prime minister resigned verbally. The proposal on the confidence vote and the resignation of the prime minister were not discussed by the assembly at this session. Since it was necessary to observe the required procedure, it was concluded that the assembly -- that at the next assembly session should be scheduled as soon as possible and that decisions will be made and the resignation of the prime minister should be discussed first in relation to the vote of confidence for the government."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the question because there was a sight translation going on of the document that was read out fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the interpreters didn't hear your question because it overlapped with your reading of the transcript -- the reading -- reading of the minute.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to say, end of quotation. The quotation was recorded properly but my question was: Does Professor Djeric remember that on the basis of the Law on the Government or some other piece of legislation, it was not possible to vote about the government at the same session where MPs would submit proposals of their own, or could one acknowledge the resignation of the prime minister at that particular session? It had to be the next session of parliament that had to be awaited.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that legal basis. I mean, I do not remember that. However, what I do know and what I claim is that it wasn't that I only submitted this resignation verbally as is stated here. What was requested was that I sign this. And I did sign it. It was a resignation in writing. There is TV footage of that and there are other recordings, too, so all of this can be confirmed or corroborated. So I said that and I signed it. So it was submitted in writing. All the conditions were there at that point in time to have the resignation received. Why that was not the case, well, maybe it was due to this opinion that was just voiced now, that the assembly did not have the right to do it at that session. However, I know my it was imperative from a legal point of view not to drag things out any further. The prime minister's resignation should have been received. It was done only at the next session, but a prime minister designate was not appointed. No preparations were carried out from that point of view, although everything had been clear. That assembly session could not have been scheduled without having the name of the new prime minister designate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that you're right, only in part. It is true that you submitted your resignation in writing in November but that was the 1st of November. It was the next session at the -- on the 23rd and 24th of November.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please call up P1362 now. Page 23 in Serbian, please; and page 12 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we please take a look at this now. It's the third paragraph in Serbian. [As read] "A long time ago I" -- so on and so forth. These are Premier Djeric's words. [As read] "A long time ago, five months ago, in May, in late May, I raised the issue of the work of the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Justice." It's around the middle, the third paragraph. [As read] "A long time ago, five months ago, in May, in late May, I raised the issue of the work of the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Justice. We've been having problems ever since. Since then the government has not been functioning and since then a sword has been hanging above the government's head. Since then, all work has been impossible," so on and so forth. Do you remember that you had verbalized that at this session?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember -- well, each and every individual word. But I do allow for this, that this is what I said, because this is the essence of those problems, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, I'm a bit confused, because you say that it was late in May that you brought up the question of the Ministry of Interior and the Ministry of Justice but that you, nevertheless, suggested that the minister start working. 5587, that's the 65 ter number that we looked at a moment ago. So it's not that you were quite resolute as far as the Ministry of Interior was concerned at the end of May; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, since then, I had intensively been giving these ministers certain instructions, to make sure that there is rule of law, to make sure that they observe the law, because, as ministers, they are directly in charge of that, you see?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are going to different consultations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There is no French. Yes, there was something wrong with the French microphone. But we can continue. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I focussed on them and the government focussed on them because of the intensive media campaign. I mean, world journalists were writing about the situation there, you know. Many things were being written, and I cannot check anything. I can get information through ministers and certain ministries along with all the other problems that are there. Every now and then you read something in the world press. Certain political interventions by diplomats, secretaries of state, and so on and so forth. So it is only natural that you have to react on the basis of all of that; that is to say, you focus your attention on that and you take all of this very seriously. Everything that is being written. You see? Very seriously. And you try to ensure legality. You try to make sure that international conventions are not being violated, that there is no unlawful conduct towards the civilian population, prisoners of war, et cetera, because that was our obligation to observe international regulations. At a very early stage, the government wrote up instructions on the treatment of prisoners of war, the status of the civilian population, and so on. As a matter of fact, the government had this translated into the English language and this was sent to international organisations so that they could supervise this. This was done institutionally, but certain ministries were asked to ensure that this happened. However, what was noticed at that point in time was that, in particular, these two minister, the minister of justice and the minister of the interior, who are key ministers, and also the ministry of the military that has more contact with the commander of the army, I mean, they were the ones that were particularly supposed to work on this. I'm saying, quite simply, that from the very outset I had to deal with these ministries and look at what happened? They just leave. And then I'd hear this talk, that they were taking care of their own profits, running their own businesses, you see? And so on and so forth. And all of this had a negative effect on other ministers, on the work of the government as a whole. So from the very outset, in a certain way, as soon as these questions were raised, as soon as ministries were asked to work on these matters, they started, you know, they started behaving in an opportunistic way. A bit. That's what the problem was. Then they went to seek protection. They went to consult and asked how they were supposed to work. They consulted someone else. They did not consult the prime minister. They did not consult the government that was giving them their tasks. Most often they went to see the political leadership and the leadership of the assembly, you know. They thought that that is where they were supposed to be told, how they are supposed to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We need to leave this document briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to see the transcript of Professor Djeric's testimony in Krajisnik. It is 65 ter 22479, page 27146. 65 ter 22479; page 27146. This is 5. Could we have page 6, the next one. [In English] Next page, please. [Interpretation] 270, and we need 27146 instead. The whole page, 101. This is 56 and we need 46 instead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Judge Orie asks you if you ever received answers to your questions, and your answer was -- just one moment. 27146. Please bear with me. It should be line 9.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid this is not the same page. Lines 3 to 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you say -- the Judge asked you if you received written reports from Stanisic concerning the issues of property and personal safety for citizens. [As read] [In English] "At the time that I was in office I kept requesting from the -- from the time in June when the government was formed, from June to October, I asked information on several occasions from that department, information on various issues. "Judge Orie: And did you ever receive a written report on it? "A. Sometimes I did; sometimes it took a while. Sometimes they would be detailed. Sometimes they would be quite brief." [Interpretation] So you did receive reports, but sometimes it took a while. On other occasions, they were detailed, and some were short. Do we agree, Professor Djeric, that the main purpose of work of that ministry is to suppress or prevent crimes, and in case there are crimes that have not been prevented, reports need to be submitted, criminal reports, to the prosecutor's offices?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. It is standard procedure that the ministry should work, study cases, and forward them to the prosecutors to bring charges. But some important information that the ministry was supposed to provide is something I did not receive. I did not. Experts could study that in order to establish what kind of information the Ministry of Interior sent to the government and what kind of information they sent to the president. The information discussed here was routine information. But as for important information, in my opinion, only the man number one received them -- received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go back to the old document. 65 ter 34, or P1362. We saw it a moment ago. While we are waiting, Professor Djeric, since there were reports from the Ministry of Interior sent to the government which arrived late, that still had nothing to do with the kind of information they sent to the prosecution. These are two separate matter: Keeping the prime minister informed and submitting criminal reports to prosecution offices. That's -- these are two separate things.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are two different processes. That is normal. I am not disputing that. What is important here was that the ministry needed to inform the government regularly, not the prime minister, but the government, and we didn't have that. If I didn't receive any reports, there was nothing for me to discuss at a -- government sessions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 25 in the Serbian and 13 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which is your contribution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date is the 23rd and 24th of October -- of November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, you say the following: "The prime minister" -- well, let me find that. I'll read it out and I hope we'll find it. [As read] "The prime minister is to be -- is told of having done many things such as fighting for power. But the prime minister was also inputted as fighting against the president of the republic. And I hope it is clear to the republican president, the prime minister is trying -- is doing his utmost to strengthen the position of the head of state through the institutions of the system in favour of rule of law. It is it wrong to think that a head of state can be strengthened by any other means or that the prime minister has different political views or an agenda of his own. Everything comes from the same centre. Everyone saying that should know that things come from a centre. The PM has no other agenda unless some people think that the prime minister was against the departure of planes, as I, indeed, was." Do you recall that in Geneva I was put under pressure and had to agree to our aviation being dislocated to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and that it wasn't only the prime minister but the government and the people refused it? That is the reference to the planes in this text.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to study this a bit more carefully. The planes reference is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the middle of the middle of the middle paragraph. "The prime minister" -- yes. "The prime minister ..." The end of the second paragraph. "It is wrong to think," et cetera, et cetera. And the paragraph ends with: "... against the departure of planes." I was, indeed, against that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go into such matters at all. A lot of things can be found in this paragraph. I really can't recall it all. But I didn't go into that, the issue of the planes, et cetera. It was a matter of high politics that Mr. Karadzic decided on, and I had nothing to do with that. Nothing. And the government did not state any position in that regard. This seems to be a mishmash. Maybe I thought that rumours were being spread against the prime minister, et cetera. Some areas in particular were upset about the planes leaving the air force. So it created an avalanche of resistance against the government as a whole. But I had nothing against that. I did not state my position. I did not participate in such talks. In terms of such issues, I had no purview. It was a matter much international agreements and their implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you enumerate --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply enumerate the things that were said against me. It seems that there was an attempt to shift the burden of responsibility on my back, and I had nothing to do with it, and I was still reading the paragraph you read out. It was in the spirit of my wish to have a -- a rule of law and a legal state. I believe then, as I do now, that any government or body of authority makes sense only if the state is functioning at the basis of rule of law. If there is no rule of law, it is not for public good. It is for public evil. That was the tone of my remarks. You said I was against the president, or that I had -- had a difference of opinion. That is true. There was a divergence of opinion between me and Mr. Krajisnik and Karadzic on many things. But when it came to fighting for certain elementary rights of the people there were no differences, as was the case in many other things. It also had to do with their understanding of rights and obligations. They were there people who said, Let's leave it now for the time being. This is not the right time. We'll deal with it tomorrow and so on and so forth. Usually such people do not really have any kind of feeling for legal logic or the thrust of time [as interpreted]. Time is irreversible. Once it's gone, it's gone. There were many people in our authorities that mixed irresponsibility with dilettantism. There weren't just one or two but more. However, such people could not be accorded influence over important matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: An intervention for the transcript. The witness said "the arrow of time" and not "thrust of time."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was trying to illustrate that the lapsing of time, past, present, future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor Djeric, was I not acting in accordance with better safe than sorry? I was overly cautious in many regards.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't discuss that now. It is your position. You can put your own position to this Court. It is possible that you thought along those lines, but I kept warning you of the need to have a functioning authority, effective authority. That is why I kept insisting on the two ministries and the two ministers, not to shelter them, that they do not enjoy the political backing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, may I ask for additional time, as this is the most important witness from the top echelons of leadership in the first couple of years of war in the Republika Srpska than Professor Djeric. I believe everyone will benefit from his clarifications of events. Please bear that in mind. We do have his amalgamated statement as his testimony in other cases, but I will mostly rely on my and his words from back then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You'll still have an hour, about an hour. But do you need more?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Excellency. Luckily neither Mr. Djeric, nor Mr. Mandic, nor anyone else were charged before this Tribunal. I was. And the Prosecution know very well what conclusions they want to draw from Professor Djeric's testimony, and they acted quite unfairly in amalgamating his statement, citing only Mr. Djeric's dissatisfaction, which I shared, by the way, I was dissatisfied with the conditions, but through such selection of material, it is suggested that I was an autocrat in favour of crimes, et cetera. This is a key testimony, and I would kindly ask for more time. I proposed that all transcripts of Professor Djeric's testimony be admitted where he discussed a number of different things. It was not approved and that is why I have to go through all these topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was why the Chamber allowed you four hours. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction for the transcript. I said that they selected such material from Professor Djeric's statements, picturing his dissatisfaction and conditions which I shared. I shared my dissatisfaction with the government, and as things stand in the transcript now, it seems I was the only one who was dissatisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have the remainder of today and half an hour tomorrow morning. That means you have an additional hour. But from now on, I would like you to be focussed on the relevant issues to your indictment. We'll take a break now for an hour and resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor Djeric, without going into who is right or who is wrong, let us now try and be consistent with the old Latin proverb "audiatur et altera pars." Now, can we have a look in this document at page 27 in Serbian. And page 14 in English. Let us see what one of the ministers that was being criticised is saying, and I am referring to Mr. Mandic. He says: [As read] "Mr. President, deputies, it was not my intention to speak immediately, but I would like to say to the people what is going on in the government and how the prime minister leads the ministers and the government. However, I would only like to mention that the conclusion from the last session of the assembly was that all the ministers and the prime minister should submit in writing their activity reports. These will be circulated to this esteemed gathering so that you can give your own assessment of the work of the prime minister and other ministers. "I am asking you now if you are in possession of these documents. No, are you not. I would now like to inform you that all the ministers did submit these to the prime minister ten days ago. In my view, the prime minister found it more important to take part in an election campaign than to circulate these documents to you so that we can evaluate the work of every minister and ministry at the government meeting. "Deputies, I assure you that we have never done this in the last seven months. Not a single meeting of the government discussed the work of the Ministry of Justice and administration or, say, that of the Ministry of Interior, both of which have been referred to here. What we are faced here with is there is apparently discord how policies are pursued, both policies of the state and policies in general." Do you remember Mandic saying this at the assembly session?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which session?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The same one on the 23rd and 24th November, 1992, when you resigned.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean when my resignation was accepted. Well, look, it is well known how a government operates and how it reports to the assembly. Everybody knows how this mechanism worked. From time to time, the government submits a report to the assembly who oversees its work. That's as far as this is concerned, and this is what we did at every session of the assembly. Every time I took to the floor in the assembly were, in a way, a method of reporting on the work of the government. Now as for specific ministries, it was very difficult to work with the gentleman mentioned herein because it was said then that he cannot look for any kind of excuses. His job was to take care and to lead the ministry, not to do all other kinds of things, and it was also his duty to report to the government. However, the -- these minutes reflect that this gentleman was often absent and there was always someone who appeared as his substitute. What he was doing in actual fact, I don't know. So who can he blame? Because it's obvious that he has some kind of invisible support from some quarters. The only one he can blame is the prime minister, so it's quite clear. And this story about the air force that we heard earlier all were also part of the game that was aimed against the prime minister. When you have a people at war, particularly if you have a majority involved, and when you have an international decision to ground all the planes and move them to Serbia, he feels an existential fear in such circumstances. And when you want to destroy someone in a political manner, you resort to such games. To put it simply, this gentleman is wrong. This is his version of events. He always sought excuses in some technicalities, whereas his ministry and he, himself, as the minister as always being on the agenda as the one who were criticised all the time. Now, speaking of all these issues, this is the key problem, and the problem is that these gentlemen enjoyed political support from somewhere, and that is what kept them in power. That is, Mr. Karadzic, why I left. After that, Mico Stanisic was reinstated as the minister of the interior in December 1993. That cannot be done without someone's support. I let this other person be appointed to some diplomatic post, et cetera. So as I said, they had political support from the political leadership and that is why they behaved in the way they did. This is where I think lies the key reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the question was whether you remember Mandic saying the part that Mr. Karadzic had read out. Do you remember Mr. Mandic said this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No -- no doubt about it. This is the last session that I attended when my resignation was accepted. And I think that was the one held in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Either in the Prijedor or in Zvornik, but this one was on the 23rd of November.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was on the 31st of October, in Prijedor, or maybe it was the 1st November, actually, when I resigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now two more questions unrelated to this document. You said that there were always some substitutes who attended in their place. Did you draw up any schedule as to who can stand in for a minister if he is prevented from attending?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were deputies who would act as substitutes but that could only happen in exceptional circumstances. That cannot become a regular practice. I would also like to make reference to the vice prime minister for internal policies, who directly co-ordinated the minister of judiciary, and the minister of the interior, and so on. But he simply complained all the time that he cannot get hold of these gentlemen at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A while ago, you said that this gentleman and his ministry was constantly being criticised. Can I find this somewhere in the minutes of the meeting of the government, specifically on the session when his ministry was discussed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can. You can review the minutes of the meeting of the government. You can see what the agenda was, which items were discussed and debated pertaining to which ministers, and you can see who the attendees were. So often, very often, someone else attended instead of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You met very frequently, almost every day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, yes. Later on, not so often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since all the minutes from the assembly, the government, and the Presidency have been admitted into evidence, we are not going to waste any time more today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 27 in Serbian and 14 in English of this same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, in the middle, it says: [As read] "I have to inform you, since I have been put on the spot, that Mr. Stanisic and I - you all probably know everything about us - how useful is each one of us, how committed to our work we are, how much effort we have put into it, and how much has been done in the last seven months. I will only inform you briefly that at our last five or six sessions, out of 100 agenda items, 90 concerned the judiciary and administration. The dozen or so of us from the Ministry of Justice and administration did as much as we could, respected you, the representatives of the local authorities, in our endeavour to set up from scratch the judicial organs, administration, correctional facilities, and misdemeanour courts. To what extent we succeeded and whether someone else could do a better job, it is up to you to judge on the basis of our activity reports and other documents. "I assure you, however, that the work of individual ministries is not being questioned here, but the leadership relationship of the prime minister who criticised the work of the assembly, i.e., you, the president of the state, who does not agree with the work of Mandic and Stanisic because we are not his private ministers. You know that under the constitution judges are appointed by the assembly and that during an imminent threat of war they are appointed by the state Presidency. "The prime minister and his deputy insisted that this be debated by the government and that we discuss individual judges. I did not agree with this because this is a matter for the grass roots and the assembly. The executive authority cannot decide on the appointment of officials to the -- in the judiciary. I objected to that. At one of the meetings that I did not attend, but the minutes are available, the government adopted a decision and elected several judges. Can you believe it? The government actually elected several judges. This is on record. "Naturally, I explained it to the prime minister that this is not how it works. That the prime minister and the government cannot decide on matters like. This disagreements ensued. I will explain to you later, as this is only a reply, that an agreement occurred at the personal level but -- because it is neither up to the government nor me to judge the work of the president of the state or the assembly president. My job is to stick to it and to implement your policies." So as they say, "audiatur et altera pars," let's hear the other said. This is what Mandic says about this issue. You listened to this and I would like to hear what you say to this. Did the government appoint judges?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning all the questions that you raised here, I'm going to respond by referring to several points. First of all, I didn't have any personal disagreement with the ministers. I said a minute ago that I didn't have any disagreement with the president, the Speaker of the parliament, or any other officials from the political authorities. Gentlemen, I told you a minute ago that this is what I said, and this was recorded in the transcript from this assembly. I said on that occasion that the president and I shared the same view when it came to the fight of the people for their rights. I would have been the happiest man on the planet had it been possible for this to be accomplished without a war. However, at that time, I was in favour of that, but what I think is extremely important is that I never perceived the rights of my people to be something to be exercised at the expense of other peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was always in favour of equality. Therefore, I assume -- or, actually, not assume. I know for sure that Mr. Karadzic was on the same wavelength at that time. Therefore, there couldn't have been any disagreements regarding this matter, including with the ministry. So this gentleman was simply offended for being picked on all the time, and he is trying to disqualify and derogate the prime minister. Now, the background of all this is that Mr. Mandic never complied with the decision of the government to submit a report on the prisoners, on how the civilian population was treated, et cetera, because that was one of his tasks. And also on war crimes. So he was supposed to submit a report to the government, and the ministry received this conclusion from the government at the beginning of June, and that was their task. But the problem is that I didn't receive it. Therefore, this is the context that I, as the prime minister, had to exert some pressure on them as ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He says --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. About the judges. Listen, it's not up to the government. The government may have debated this but only on the basis of a proposal from the ministry. In other words, if this really happened, it was his ministry that had prepared it for the government. His ministry. Nobody made that up. I couldn't have put that on the agenda. It could have been done by his ministry alone. But, as usual, he was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we're listening to the other side as well. So it seems to me that Mr. Mandic is trying to say that they worked properly but that your objection in terms of his not respecting the work of the prime minister or collective -- well, is it correct that the work of the parliament was based on submissions by the Ministry of Justice, 95 per cent; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, depends how you measure it. When a government comes into being, and when you have to have some kind of institutionalisation, then you have to have proper legislation and you have to have a Ministry of Justice and a public administration that function properly. Now what percentage that was? I mean -- well, I'm not denying that his desk officers, his bureaucrats at the ministry prepared all of that, so that was coming in, but the minister was not there to state his views in terms of the main work of the government; and that is the report, the report to prepare a report, about everything that was happening on the ground to the -- the extent to which there was rule of law and the extent to which this was highlighted. After all, there are minutes, and there are jobs involved. I think that these gentlemen and -- went out there and consulted with the political leadership, and they were dragging their feet a bit. In the president, they found a man who thought that time heals everything, but you know what? I think that that is this not the case. Not this kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, please let me finish. I think that you did not assess the political situation. Had you punished what was supposed to be punished from day one, later on, things would not have happened. Worse things. So I left, and the problems remained, Mr. Karadzic. So I left. I tried to persuade you. I told you about all of this, but all the problems remained. And what happened, happened. I am not going to go into all of that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have English page 15 and Serbian page 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, again, is speaking here, but I tried to abridge it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this page 29? Yes, it could be there. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now -- just a moment, please. So it is the first third. [As read] "I'm not a sycophant. I struggle and I work as best I can. And that's the way I'm going to be. If this assembly says that I am not the right person for the judiciary and the administration, which was not the case last time, Radovan Karadzic and Momo Krajisnik did not stop me from leaving the position of minister. It was you. You voted. You did not want me to be a minister without portfolio. If you remember, I think that was in Bijeljina. There are not any personal reasons involved. It was your decision, and you thought that I was supposed to finish what I started, which is what I've tried to do, with all possible means." And so on and so forth. So now there's a lot of hearsay involved, a lot of intrigue. [As read] "Did any of you ever see any reports from us stating whose mistake this was? Momo Mandic's or Branko Djeric's?" And now a bit further down, Mr. Djeric says -- it's this last paragraph. Mr. Djeric says that he advocates the rule of law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just wait. Next page for the English. Yes. [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [As read] "Mr. Djeric says that he is in favour of rule of law and the constitution. Several times at government meetings, I made some critical remarks stating that the government cannot take over the powers of the Presidency and the assembly. Several times we adopted governments -- decisions made by the government establishing public institutions. All of that is done by the assembly, and you know that full well. Certain officials were appointed by the government which is supposed to be done by the assembly. Now, who is interfering in whose work, the government in the assembly's work or the assembly in the government's work? I kept saying that this is not right. Therefore, I was no good and I could not be part of Djeric's government." So he says that these are doctrinary and professional differences in terms of what the powers involved were and that there were some appointments that he complained about at government sessions and that this led to some personal animosities between you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, this is ridiculous, you know? This is just empty talk. He's making excuses. He's trying to move onto a different track altogether. This is not correct. How can the government take over the powers of the assembly when the -- when the assembly is there all the time, when the president of the assembly is there all the time? Had Mr. Krajisnik protested who was in charge of the assembly then, well, then, that would have been a different story because it was for him to say what the assembly was doing and what the government was doing. The government wasn't doing no such thing. The government could have prepared certain documents for the assembly, but for the government to perform the functions of the assembly, that did not happen. That is not true. Quite simply, he is making excuses here. Excuses for himself. The main thing is here is, and I underline that, the government from the beginning of the June was supposed to do that, namely, the ministry was supposed to submit a report to the government about people being taken prisoner, about the treatment of the civilian population, and so on and so forth. They had to submit a report because the government had already worked out all the necessary regulations and they started operating. We never received that, all the way up until the month of October. It was only in October that the report arrived from the Ministry of Justice, and the government acted on the basis of that report. There was some unlawful detention facilities that were then disbanded and so on. So from the beginning of June, until this period of time, this kept going on and on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can just add one thing here, that, often, these two ministers, and this one, Mandic, often went to see the leadership, the leadership that consisted, first of all, of Karadzic, Krajisnik and Koljevic. Biljana and I -- Biljana Plavsic and I were sort of opposition there. That's why these gentlemen didn't like me or Plavsic, and they kept -- they kept trying to find a way out with the top political leadership. I said this once somewhere, that Mr. Karadzic was not against punishing crimes, but he kept postponing that for later. Do you understand that? And I asked for punishment to be meted out straight away. So that is the actual conflict with this minister and the other one, and that is the core of the matter. No wonder the problem escalated in this period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get to that. We have documents. We have your documents and my documents, but now I wanted us to look at page 31. So let us hear the third other side, so there's not only just one other side that is there. There's the prime minister, the premier and then also -- well, look at this, page 31. [As read] "I would like," it's the last paragraph. This is Mr. Stanisic who is speaking there. If necessary, we can go back so you can see -- we can see in the English version that it's Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English it should be page 17. Page 17.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the English page please be returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, for the benefit of the interpreters it's better to have both English version and B/C/S version on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "I would appreciate ..." So Mr. Stanisic says at this very same assembly session: [As read] "I would appreciate it if some of the gentlemen here were to say I insisted, first of all, as the minister of the interior ... there is no rule of law without laws on the basis of which the Ministry of the Interior can work. The Ministry of Interior cannot work on the basis of emotions. We will then turn into a mob committing acts of violence against its own people. I don't want to do that. I reject that. That has nothing to do with the rule of law. The -- when there is rule of law, the police force works and it's role is in the rule of law. Actually, that of the Ministry of the Interior is a preventative one: To report crimes and not to arrest and beat people. It is not for the police to do other work. There are other organs responsible for that when there is rule of law. I am in favour of rule of law and I insist that the police act in such a way or otherwise I will not accept this role." Do you remember that that was the position; and do you remember that there was a certain lack of understanding there, that, perhaps, the police was wrong, according to the prime minister, but if they submit reports to the Office of the Prosecutor, then they have actually carried out their basic function; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at page 83. I smiled a bit when I read your characterisation of Mr. Ostojic in the amalgamated statement. Do you know, Mr. Djeric, that even in western parliaments there's a man who is called the whip and that is the man from a particular political party who is following the way in which MPs vote. That even exists in the British parliament and that is exactly the way you portrayed Mr. Ostojic. May he rest in peace. He is deceased now.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not have in mind the parliament or the position of a party leader in mind. I was actually thinking of Attila and he actually wanted to portray himself in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, a zealous man from the party?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, zealous, and he liked power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please let me find this now. But he is insisting on the following now. If this is page 83, it says up here "Velibor Ostojic." It says: [As read] "But therefore he insists on the following." Can we have the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: English page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. In English, it is 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's the middle of the penultimate paragraph, where it says "Prijedor." [As read] "Therefore I insist on the following. Gentlemen, deputies, in Prijedor you can concluded that you should ask the government for a report and to have the ministries' report included in this report. That was your decision. I observe that decision and submit a report to the prime minister because I want people to know how much I did, how much of it is my responsibility, and how much I may be criticised and how much I may be awarded. This decision was not observed. "I therefore ask the following question: Whose minister am I? I do not accept that I am the prime minister's minister. I am a minister in the government of Republika Srpska, and I am a minister of this state, and I am a minister who is accountable to this parliament, just as you are accountable to the people. That is the system of responsibility in place. As part of that, I protest because the government's report and the ministries's report were not presented, based on the decision you adopted in Prijedor." So he claims that he submitted the report too. Do you remember that they certainty you these reports and perhaps because of your resignation or something else, you did not forward them to the assembly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time, the government looks at the work of each and every ministry. They are asking for reports to be submitted and then they discuss these reports. It is not customary for the assembly or anyone else to discuss a ministry. They discuss the entire government. They ask the entire government for a report. The assembly could not have a debate without a report, you see? What ask is focussed here is bureaucracy, red tape. We are not looking at bureaucracy here now. That's not the main point. What I discussed is what really mattered. As for Velibor Ostojic's statement, this is a typical statement from party positions so that he could support these other ministers in this way or that. I hope that you have understood the core of the problem here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 117 in the Serbian and 61 of the English in the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These are Karadzic's words. Towards the bottom, he says: [As read] "I intentionally did not wish to speak until now. You heard my opinions at the deputies' club meeting yesterday. Now that this is so, I can tell you that there is no conflict between the Presidency and the prime minister. The -- I hold the prime minister in high regard and we kindly asked him for the third time to accept the mandate, and we even used our common friends. When we nominated him, we were very satisfied with the previous work of the government. However, it was our belief that we need to change something under the burden of responsibility. We simply need to start working in a different manner. Even if things were at their best, some changes still need to be made in order to accelerate things. "On this occasion, I'd like to congratulate first and foremost Mr. Djeric for what he had done this far. When we are doing something -- well, if someone has anything to say in terms of their hostility, that would be unforgivable in terms of someone sitting in the Presidency or lack of principle, as far as I can say, our relationship with Mr. Djeric is at the highest possible level. However, there's disbelief that things need to be changed to a certain extent. "We did discuss matters, but we did not consult about the issue of the new prime minister designate. We did not know the outcome of it all and did not want to rush ahead. When we thought about it, we wanted the Presidency to do something. I have a number of ideas. Conditions needs to be secured as well as personnel, and they all need to be talked to to see what their ideas are. Some of them will remain part of the government if they so wish, and, if possible, to do it within the next fortnight." Do you remember that my position concerning you was always as stated here and I stated it publicly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did say so, was your opinion about me, and that is not in dispute, your opinion of me as a person. But this touches upon other issues that I wanted to resolve as the prime minister, and they were not resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 121 in the Serbian and 63 in the English version to see what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djeric, the paragraph beginning with, [As read] "At the same time..." It is from the session of 23rd/24th October. [As read] "At the same time, I want to thank you for your co-operation. I think this co-operation was ample and within the limits of possible co-operation. After all, there is no need to prolong it very much. We have to find a designate, form a new government, and let it work. "In offering my resignation I wanted certain changes and that we make certain turnarounds on behalf of the people and for the people. And, at this moment, although I could have withdrawn my resignation and further complicated things, I do not wish to do so, for the very reason that we must do everything for our people, despite what my dignity would allow me or not. Thank you." So you could observe that I delayed the consultations and election of the new prime minister designate, expecting that tensions would ease at this particular session and that you would withdraw your resignation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot go into what you expected or thought would happen and what was realistic or not, particularly in view of the fact that I resigned in writing. People did try to convince me to withdraw the resignation and maybe some people counted on it but I refused. As you can see, my position was resolute and I said that it was out of the question. There was nothing to wait any further. A new prime minister designate had to be appointed, and things should have moved ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you believe that someone would try to talk you into withdrawing your resignation without prior consultation with me, once they have acquired my approval?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot speculate about that. But, yes, there were people who suggested it to me, presenting it as the only way out, as the only solution. But I did not accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next have 65 ter 125, which is D440.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the 15th Session of the Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the circumstances of an immediate threat of war held on the 16th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 6th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Agenda item 1, the question of Dr. Nikola Koljevic's participation in the work of the Presidency. Apparently he was dissatisfied with his perform and that he could no longer endure physically or psychologically and stressed that he was having family problems.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at page 2 to see what Professor Djeric said. The second paragraph from the top. [As read] "Professor Djeric pointed out that the results of the work are significant, irrespective of the self-criticism by Professor Koljevic. No further improvisations should be tolerated in the course of work. The Presidency should -- the Presidency has no division of labour and we need to establish connections with the different ministries. Working bodies of the Presidency should be set up," and he disagreed that little was done by the Presidency. And it says: [As read] "Dr. Branko Djeric pointed out that the dominant policy of the Presidency was one of not upsetting people. He pointed out that the accommodation of the government and the Presidency was also a problem." So you, Professor Djeric, suggested that the different government departments establish closer ties with the Presidency, and probably you had in mind the Ministry of Interior and Defence rather than the Ministry of Economic Affairs or Forestry, for example.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I meant. I simply had in mind ties between people. That there are departments that should be asked for opinions and that there should be consultations.
