Members of the Presidency cannot hold the posts of ministers, and often people saw their role in exactly that way. That is why I discussed ties, as there should be in any system. There is such -- there are such things as co-ordination and communication. That was the thrust of my argument. I was prompted to say that because things -- such serious matters should not be improvised, and of course there will be upset people along the away. There are always private interests or interests of other kinds involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that following your contribution and after the meeting, we talked vice-president Koljevic into staying in the Presidency and we assigned him the mandate of the minister of foreign affairs, and on behalf of the government, Mr. Buha acted in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that he was dissatisfied with something although I don't know what it was. In any case, he was a member of the Presidency who expressed his dissatisfaction, and you should know more about that, and probably that is why you offered him another position involving foreign relations. There was a ministry of foreign affairs, so I can't say that I agreed to his new position. We had a minister of foreign affairs, but you did find a position for him within foreign relations and you calmed him down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that he was dissatisfied with his own contribution and that any institution would have departments in charge of foreign relations? There are committees for foreign relations in parliaments. There are similar parts in the government. And if we have a Presidency, then it's the president who is in charge of foreign relations or there is a person who is designated that role.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not in dispute, but I can only say that I don't know what it was that he objected to. Apparently he was dissatisfied, but you know better what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have a look at 65 ter 1118. It seems to be P3758. Professor Djeric, did you order the Ministry of Justice, either orally or in writing, to submit a report about the situation with prisons?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an official conclusion of the government early on. Perhaps in June or late May. We asked for a report. We could see media reporting, and there was a lot of pressure on the Serb side. Foreign diplomats made statements, as well as secretaries of state. As far as I remember, the government even issued a decision to address the ministers of foreign affairs of some important countries, in particular, the five permanent members of the Security Council and as well as the organisation of European Co-operation and Development. That is what prompted the government to ask for a report from the ministry so that we would know what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the government did not receive certain reports it wanted and reacted to something that was made public internationally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, something in that regard. The competent ministry had to prepare a report and it was one of the main preoccupations or duties of the government to monitor such matters in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at this letter of mine sent to you on the 7th of August. [As read] "Dear Mr. Prime minister, I hereby deliver to you copies of the reports on the situation in Manjaca and Bileca prisons that I just received. In regard to these reports, I have sent a letter to Mr. Cornelio Sommaruga, president of the ICRC, and to General Ratko Mladic. "Based on these reports, I expect the government to take prompt action through the ministries of justice and the interior to improve the living conditions in the prisons in our territory housing -- run by civilian authorities." Do you recall this letter?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't put this in any context. I don't remember it but I have no reason to doubt that this was so. The government had already been working on it, and you sent this letter quite late on the 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, because it had to do with the report received from Mr. Sommaruga.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You were in charge of such affairs in the Presidency, perhaps alone or in co-operation with Kalenic, but you were in charge of it. Foreign relations were in your hands, the hands of the Presidency, in a way. I don't want to go back to it, but the ministers also saw you frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please bear with me. Were you able to observe that in the international community reports and diplomatic statements there were inaccurate statements or information supplanted by the other side?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only say anything about that once I have received a report from our side. It is only then that I could discuss what was correct or not. That is why that was the crux of the problem. You, in other words, intervened as the president on the 7th of August, whereas the government reacted as early as, say, the 7th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that Professor Koljevic, in terms of your criticism of Stanisic and Mandic, sided with you, more or less?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nikola could switch sides easily. That's the kind of person he was. And, ultimately, that was the reason of his dissatisfaction and why you tried to calm him down, to appease him, with the positions you created for him. I did not see Professor Koljevic as a stable statesman. He struck me more as a university drama professor. That's how I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, literature, Shakespearology?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I won't speak ill of the dead, but when it comes to statehood affairs, things have to be done properly and quickly because time is irreversible and things have to be taken more seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I please have now 1D04195, which is D1672. Do you remember that I set up a commission to investigate the allegations concerning Mr. Mandic, Mr. Stanisic, and Mr. Tomo Kovac and their involvement in illegal activities, and I appointed Mr. Koljevic the chairman of that commission? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was on the 23rd of October, 1993. We're going to look at it now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D04195, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that was in 1993, I'm not a competent person to speak about it because I left in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But given that some allegations persisted afterwards, the person who criticised Mandic, and he was a highly placed official, I asked you to investigate all these allegations, and believe me, after a long investigation, Professor Koljevic submitted a report that these allegations were baseless in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot speak about this. Except that I can say that at first glance I can only establish a link between this and the subsequent reappointment of Mico Stanisic as minister of the interior, which happened towards the end of 1993. Probably the late Professor Koljevic had some reasons why he acted in the way he did. The fact is that Mico Stanisic was appointed minister of the interior for the second term of office in late 1993, and you don't need any special scientific measures. You don't have to be a brain surgeon to perceive that there is a connection between this and the future events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that after the fall of your government, the new prime minister designate did not take either Mandic or Stanisic to become members of the government, whereas Stanisic was reinstated only after the report submitted by Professor Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a fact. As far as I can remember, that's how things happened. They had no place in the government after I had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now deal a little bit about -- with the relationship between our authorities and citizens of Republika Srpska of other ethnicities. And for that purpose, can we please look at D90, or 65 ter 20. This is the assembly session of 28th [as interpreted] March, 1992, a few hours after the acceptance of the Lisbon Agreement, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Now, as for the dates, I can only take your word for it, and I -- I -- I agree that if you say so, it was several hours after the Lisbon Agreement was accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic may have been about to correct the transcript on that, but it's not the 28th March. It's 18 March as we can see on the stenograph before us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I did say the 18th, but I concede that. Can we have page 22 in Serbian and 16 in English. 22 in Serbian and 16 in English. But it could be 22 in the actual document and not necessarily in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's find the portion that begins: [As read] "We are going now," or "We shall." We have it in English. It's the penultimate paragraph, which begins with: "We shall ..." I'm going to read it. Just a moment, please. Here we have it. Thank you very much to the Registry. [As read] "We shall now have to establish a full structure of government on the ground, because this is our duty to the people who live there, Serbs, Muslims, or Croats, so that we can secure peace. Then, through negotiations, we shall try to achieve the maximum requirements. It is not clear whether this will be the situation of the 1974 constitution or not, but, at this stage, our strategy is to start dividing jurisdictions." Do you agree, Professor Djeric, that all of us in the leadership, including yourself, shared the same opinion that each constituent unit will have a certain percentage of Serbs, Croats, and Muslims living there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that. This was taken into account and we strived towards preserving the equality of people who remained in their original places of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that an idea was to provide reciprocal protection of collective rights, whereas individual lives of Serbs, Croats, and Muslims would be totally equal?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, and that would constitute a basis on which the government operated. In that context I have to say a few things that were adopted as such at the very beginning. For example, the government suspended the privatisation processes that had been initiated until such time when everything became normal and in which everybody would be able to participate. That was a very serious thing. Secondly, the government issued a ban on the possession of vacant flats because these flats should remain the possession of their original owners even though they were empty and that it can only be occupied on a temporary basis with the accompanying cataloguing of the belongings that are found in such flats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 66 of this same document. And it's page 45 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Third paragraph in Serbian. [As read] "I think that the council of ministers will have to work around the clock to be able to prepare some additional laws to establish the SDK and so forth. We shall announce our withdrawal from the MUP, not to mention that we have already obtained the badges. Our police will have to act in accordance with the law. No one must be harmed, regardless of their religion or nation. Everyone must feel absolutely safe." Was that a unanimous position taken by all the relevant factors in the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs, irrespective of whether they were partisan people or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is true that this attitude and these words reflected our commitment to have all the civil, human, and all other rights be respected and that there could be no exception.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The next paragraph speaks about the maps and I say the following: [As read] "As far as the maps are concerned, the Muslims have agreed with them. It is a different matter altogether. The maps will have to be corrected. The working group would not exist if this was the final map." Do you remember that, for example, the question whether certain villages would be included or not included was a very sensitive issue and that for that purpose these working groups were established to draw these micro boundaries?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were commissions that were involved in these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As well as in other forms of analysis or examinations regarding economy and everything else contained in the Cutileiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The next paragraph reads: [As read] "That is why I ask you to do whatever is necessary to establish on the ground the de facto situation based on justice and the law, to have good and complete control of our destinies and areas, with full respect for citizens of other nationalities. That is what people will be judged by." "There will be various relocations, but nothing must be done under duress. We see that the Serbs from Livno are moving out and so forth, which is all natural a part of such a dangerous process of an intense process of reorganising a state." Do you agree that this question of the factual situation prevailing on the 18th March did not refer to a war situation because at that time we had hoped that the war was avoided on the basis of the Lisbon Agreement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree, because at that time nobody thought about war at all. Recently, I have learned how the parties had been arming themselves the whole year before the Cutileiro Plan, and I have only recently learned how people earned their pension on that basis. And this is something that I learned only lately. I never knew that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that in March there was a huge movement of Serbs from Livno once they realised that Livno would not part of the Serbian constituent unit and that they relocated themselves to the Serb-controlled areas, and this is what I mentioned in my address to the assembly.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember particularly the situation with Livno at the moment, but I do remember that at the time people were afraid and ready to migrate. But as specifically concerning Livno, I cannot remember anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that prevalent within all the three constituent groups, that they slowly started moving towards their respective territories?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot make any judgement on that matter, nor can I make any assertions to that effect. However, generally speaking, all three sides were afraid, and there was a tendency, individual tendencies, to join their respective ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 65 ter 28, which is D92. Can we have page 18 in Serbian and 21 in English. This is the assembly session, 24 to 26 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your address. But let us look at the top of the page, where we have the words of Radovan Karadzic. This is my speech, and you can see that on the previous page. And I say that: [As read] "Regrettably I have to say that in Podrinje the Muslims are not in favour of peace, except in Bijeljina and Pale where there are 20 per cent of them, because nobody is touching them, nor does anyone consider them second-rate citizens. Quite the contrary. Our state officials communicate with them with a view to convincing them that they have no reason to be afraid. Therefore, in the Serb BiH, the Serbs have accomplished their state, their freedom, and a state big enough for all. I hope that we reach in this assembly session some conclusions and decisions to further entrench this state." Do you agree that guarantees were provided for -- to the Muslims of Pale that they would not get in harm's way?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, one can understand to mean exactly that. Everybody knows that the Muslims living in Pale were respected, and I think that their will was taken into account by the local authorities at all times. So the presence of the government there was an additional guarantee to the Muslim population living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that they remained living there for as long as they wished and that they left only when the coffins with the killed Serbian soldiers started to arrive, which they felt embarrassed about and they wanted to leave?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not closely connected with these affairs, and I cannot make any comment on this. I'm -- suppose that you had more information from the local level.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 87 in Serbian and 86 in English. It's the same session. Let me find the relevant passage. Give me a moment, please. I needed 87 in Serbian and 86 in English. Here it is. It's towards the bottom. Here it is. Yes, where the cursor is. Thank you. Someone -- someone's Serbian is very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [As read] "At first we are certainly going to have that many Serbs, but I think that they will all leave their state. The Muslim state and the Croat state. In that state that we are building we have to ensure all rights for them, all the rights that we have, if they are not hostile towards us and they should lay down their weapons. In Romanija some villages are surrendering their weapons like those who live in Bijeljina and other villages. The main precondition is for them to surrender all weapons so that they can enjoy all rights." So was this not only my position but the position of all responsible people. Whoever is not shooting will enjoy rights equal to those enjoyed by any other citizen. Do you know that almost until the end of the war some villages in the Romanija area lived in peace in our republic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This position, with or without weapons, was often pointed out. I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The precondition is that they have no weapons, that they do not fight; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The precondition is for them to live in peace, not to use weapons, you know. Weapons are weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5587 is the 65 ter number. Could I please have that document. It is D422.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Today you mentioned that the government, through the ministry or the ministry through the government, proposed judges when the assembly could not meet and, therefore, in accordance with the constitution, the president appointed judges until the next assembly session.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is on the basis of the constitution: Until the assembly meets again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have page 18 now in Serbian and in English. I beg your pardon. I said 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you sent this to me, and I nominated some 18 or 20 judges, Croats and Muslims; however, when the assembly started working, I and you and all the rest - remember? - had to fight for this, for the assembly to continue appointing Muslims and Croats to institutions of the judiciary. Look at what I said about that in August: [As read] "I think that not only with regard to this proposal but in principle, I would say, look, as we said yesterday, we have to see if that person is appropriate. But, as far as other ethnicities are concerned, we have to have a percentage, a proportion participating in the municipal authorities. We have to be responsible. We are creating a state. You are the organ creating it. The state must be created swiftly and in the best way. The state must have all its elements in order to survive and to remain as a state. I cannot elaborate on this longer but I know what I'm saying. "Believe me, Alija is paying a fortune to any Serb willing to stay and work in his territory. He is begging the metropolitan bishop there and sending his people to convince him. I think that the Serb people are building a state and they know how to make a state, and because we know how to make a state we need to make it with all the elements." Do you agree that this pertains to all ethnicities in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the spirit of your speech. So it is within this subject too. You see that the government prepared that for you. The proposal included judges of all ethnic backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I nominated them and that is in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are facts that cannot be refuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the chairman is explaining the opposition voiced by MPs. He says: [As read] "Radovan, let me explain: Nobody rejects them because they are not good or because they are Muslims or Croats. Simply, we have decided to declare ourselves now because we are in a civil of war. So they will lose this number of judges, and when the war is over they will be re-elected." So you see, it was easier when I could sign your decisions rather than when they were sent to 83 MPs.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this is at the same time a reply to Mandic's letter. You know about the appointment of ministers. Now you see, don't you, that according to the constitutional law the government prepared this material for the Presidency when the assembly could not meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D02064. Can we please see that. And then page 16 in Serbian. I'm afraid we don't have the translation yet but it is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a decree of yours. While we're waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Slow down, Mr. Karadzic. Slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 16 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So here it is, the 2nd of May, 1992. As prime minister, you adopted a government decree and I'm going to read it out now. [As read] "On the basis of article such and such, there's a temporary ban on selling and buying apartments that are socially owned in the territory of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please slow down. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It's short. I don't even have to read all of this out because we're going to tender this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Already on the 2nd of May you passed a decree prohibiting the buying and selling of apartments because the situation is not regular; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation is not regular. And this would give way to illegal trade in apartments that belonged to others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And temporarily abandoned apartments could change their owners; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about that a moment ago. That was the essence. As far as I can remember, I know that at a very early stage the government passed these documents so that no citizens who lived there would be harmed. What we took in mind -- what -- what we took into account was that their rights should not be infringed upon in any way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be MFI'd. And before we are done for the day, could I just show you two more documents. They're short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D2245.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. D111. Can we have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see to which extent we agreed on basic questions pertaining to the protection of human rights.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this please be zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that on the 23rd of August --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, could you zoom in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I gave instructions based on what the government had done previously, so these are instructions. And it says up here in the preamble: [As read] "There's a widespread phenomenon that local people move into empty apartments instead of refugees and they retain the right to have several apartments. Abandoned apartments are a phenomenon of war, just like refugees are. That means that both of these things are temporary. Could the following instructions please be adhered to strictly:" And, then, it says: [As read] "Temporarily abandoned apartments can be given for provisional use to refugees only and not to local persons." Can you please take a look at this? This is a document which has already been admitted. Do you agree that the Presidency and government are working hand in hand here on protecting the rights of citizens of Muslim ethnicity, primarily?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I approve of this, but I don't understand why you had to do this if there was a government decree in place already. That is what I find interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Probably until August, I got some information to the effect that there were certain abuses, so I did not issue a decree. I issued instructions that they abide by this. Does that seem reasonable to you? Because somebody probably told me that this was a widespread phenomenon?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. If you wanted to be double sure, then, yes. But if the authorities function properly, then there were sufficient legal grounds previously in government decrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we really have to stop now? Do we have to stop now for the day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That was the last question for the day. You will have exactly -- up to half an hour tomorrow morning, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Tieger, did you have any other point?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When will we hear from you about the -- about your observation on the commencement of Defence case, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It will be filed tomorrow, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah. Tomorrow is the deadline, I think. Thank you. Yes, thank you. The hearing is now adjourned. We will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00.
